17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Any $6\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
- **II.** The matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]$ has one negative singular value.
- **III.** Any $4\times 5$ matrix $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values." :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $6\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

- Statement III is false. Since $A$ is a $4\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 4$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 4}\times {A}_{4\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 \\ -2 & -4 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4-\lambda  & -4 \\ -2 & -4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & -4 \\ -4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}0 & 4-\lambda  \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )((4-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-16)-4(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )(20-4\lambda -5\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-16)-4(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +4)-4(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +4-4) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -4)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )^{2}-1) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-1) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{2} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}

of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers.

Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by 

![](images/a9/a9edbe1fee59758c9557d95ea8f62468f9f3cb98449c437a274bdbf5c30f7dc6.svg)

Now, since

- $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and

- $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix,

then $A^T \! A$  must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.

- If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. $$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda  & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}|-4|\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ 0 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )[(5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-4)]-16(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +16)-16(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda (4-\lambda )(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

:question/math-academy-id "q-139505" :question/problem "What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )((5-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-16) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +9) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )(\lambda -1)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{1}=1\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b00be353-af3c-5697-8948-437078c60988"} {:db/id 17592186049199 :topic/id #uuid "e2d5739b-5d8f-5b44-8b7e-0b4e50252e45" :topic/knowledge-points [{:db/id 17592186203942 :knowledge-point/title "Quadratics With Positive Coefficients (After Initial Factoring)"}] :question/problem "Factor the trinomial $-4w^2-30w-50$." :question/worked-solution "We need to factor the following expression:

$$
-4w^2-30w-50
$$

First, notice that all the terms in the trinomial have a common factor of $-2$. So, we can simplify the calculation by first factoring out $-2$:

$$
-2(2w^2+15w+25)
$$

Now, we need to factor the trinomial $2w^2+15w+25$ in parentheses. To do this, we find two numbers that

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($2 \times 25 = 50$), and
- add to the linear coefficient ($15$).

Since all coefficients are positive, we only need to consider the positive factor pairs of $50$.

The positive factor pairs of $50$ are

$$
(1,50),\quad (2,25),\quad (5,10)
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(5,10)$ add to $15{:}$

$$
5+10 =15 \quad{\color{green}\checkmark}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $5w+10w$, and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2w^{2} + 15w + 25 &=  \\
2w^{2} + 5w + 10w + 25 &=  \\
2w^{2} + 10w + 5w + 25 &=  \\
(2w^{2} + 10w) + (5w + 25) &=  \\
2w(w + 5) + 5(w + 5) &=  \\
&= (2w + 5)(w + 5)
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the original trinomial factors as follows:

$$
-2(2w + 5)(w + 5)
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048375} {:db/id 17592186049023} {:db/id 17592186204183 :question/id #uuid "6079796c-07d2-5d63-bbf8-202e75124211" :question/math-academy-id "q-111850"} {:db/id 17592186204336 - 35t + 20$." :question/worked-solution "We must factor the following expression:
$-10t^2 - 35t +20$

First, notice that all the terms have a common factor of $-5$. So, we can simplify the calculation by first factoring out $-5$:

$$
-5(2t^{2} + 7t - 4)
$$

Now, we just need to factor the trinomial $2t^2 + 7t - 4$ in parentheses. To do this, we find two numbers that

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($2 \times (-4) = -8$), and
- add to the linear coefficient ($7$).

The factor pairs of $-8$ are
$(1,-8),\quad (-1,8),\quad (2,-4),\quad (-2,4)$.

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(-1,8)$ add to $7{:}$

$$
-1+8 = 8-1 = 7 \quad{\color{green}\checkmark}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $-t+8t$, and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2t^{2} + 7t - 4 &=  \\
2t^{2} - t + 8t - 4 &=  \\
(2t^{2} - t) + (8t - 4) &=  \\
t(2t - 1) + 4(2t - 1) &=  \\
&= (2t - 1)(t + 4)
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the original trinomial factors as follows:
$-5(2t - 1)(t + 4)$"} {:db/id 17592186204338 :question/id #uuid "04b8028b-be44-5d78-80c2-4a853e68e12f" :question/math-academy-id "q-225186"} {:db/id 17592186204345 :question/id #uuid "209d2ea1-5808-58c8-a9e4-f2ef5d54b4db" :question/math-academy-id "q-225279"} {:db/id 17592186203944 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203746 :question/id #uuid "81afbe63-1358-5d90-999d-4797f5f44f78" :question/math-academy-id "e-15089"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0e1a8957-9964-5eba-b5f4-b0e1dd525838" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204184 :question/id #uuid "6352e5af-8a90-5a01-85f5-71f0d126869e" :question/math-academy-id "q-111852"} {:db/id 17592186204337 :question/id #uuid "98b7e6f2-e40d-535e-a12b-3e5bd59b4957" :question/math-academy-id "q-225073"}] :knowledge-point/title "Quadratics With Negative Linear Coefficients and Positive Constants (After Initial Factoring)"} {:db/id 17592186203746 :question/id #uuid "81afbe63-1358-5d90-999d-4797f5f44f78" :question/math-academy-id "e-15089" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186203944 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0e1a8957-9964-5eba-b5f4-b0e1dd525838" :knowledge-point/title "Quadratics With Negative Linear Coefficients and Positive Constants (After Initial Factoring)"}] :question/problem "Factor the trinomial $15x^2-40x+20$." :question/worked-solution "We need to factor the following expression:

First, notice that all the terms have a common factor of $5$. So, we can simplify the calculation by first factoring out $5{:}$
$5(3x^{2} - 8x + 4)$

Now, we just need to factor the trinomial $3x^2 - 8x + 4$ in parentheses. To do this, we find two numbers that

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant (which is $3 \times 4 = 12$), and
- add to the linear coefficient (which is $-8$).

Since the linear coefficient is negative and the constant is positive, we need to consider the *negative* factor pairs of $12$.

The negative factor pairs of $12$ are

$$
(-1,-12),\quad (-2,-6),\quad (-3,-4)
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(-2,-6)$ add to $-8{:}$

$$
-2-6= -8 \quad{\color{green}\checkmark}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $-2x-6x$, and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3x^{2} - 8x + 4 &=  \\
3x^{2} - 2x - 6x + 4 &=  \\
3x^{2} - 6x - 2x + 4 &=  \\
(3x^{2} - 6x) - (2x - 4) &=  \\
3x(x - 2) - 2(x - 2) &=  \\
&= (3x - 2)(x - 2)
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the original trinomial factors as follows:
$5(3x - 2)(x - 2)$"} {:db/id 17592186204184 :question/id #uuid "6352e5af-8a90-5a01-85f5-71f0d126869e" :question/math-academy-id "q-111852"} {:db/id 17592186204337 :question/id #uuid "98b7e6f2-e40d-535e-a12b-3e5bd59b4957" :question/math-academy-id "q-225073" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186203944 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0e1a8957-9964-5eba-b5f4-b0e1dd525838" :knowledge-point/title "Quadratics With Negative Linear Coefficients and Positive Constants (After Initial Factoring)"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/id #uuid "90c7b183-e533-502b-8176-8388d1565702" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186200939} {:answer-field/id #uuid "17c3c1df-a7e2-5642-ad06-78f1c0578359" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186200940} {:answer-field/id #uuid "7af37f00-7de9-5a1f-b9ee-080fd67e4675" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186200941}] :question/problem "**Fully** factor the following trinomial.$8y^{2} - 36y + 40 =$

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186204741 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205291 :tutorial/content "When factoring a trinomial, we should always begin by factoring out any constant factors. Then, we factor whatever quadratic remains using the techniques we've studied.

For example, let's factor the following trinomial:

$$
6y^2+21y+9
$$

The first thing to notice is that all the terms have a common factor of $3$. So, we can simplify the calculation by first factoring out $3$:
$3(2y^2 + 7y + 3)$

So, our goal now is to factor the trinomial in parentheses:

$$
2y^2 + 7y + 3
$$

To do this, we find two numbers that

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($2 \times 3 = 6$), and
- add to the linear coefficient ($7$).

Also, since all coefficients are positive, we only need to consider the *positive* factor pairs of $6$.

The positive factor pairs of $6$ are

$$
(1,6),\quad (2,3)
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(1,6)$ add to $7{:}$

$$
1+6 =7 \quad{\color{green}\checkmark}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $y+6y$, and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2y^{2} + 7y + 3 = \\
2y^{2} + y + 6y + 3 &=  \\
(2y^{2} + y) + (6y + 3) &=  \\
y(2y + 1) + 3(2y + 1) &=  \\
&= (y + 3)(2y + 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the original trinomial factors as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
6y^{2} + 21y + 9 &=  \\
3(2y^{2} + 7y + 3) &=  \\
&= 3(y + 3)(2y + 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

And we're done!

we should always begin by factoring out any constant factors. Then, we factor whatever quadratic remains using the techniques we've studied.

For example, let's factor the following trinomial:

$$
6y^2+21y+9
$$

The first thing to notice is that all the terms have a common factor of $3$. So, we can simplify the calculation by first factoring out $3$:
$3(2y^2 + 7y + 3)$

So, our goal now is to factor the trinomial in parentheses:

$$
2y^2 + 7y + 3
$$

To do this, we find two numbers that

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($2 \times 3 = 6$), and
- add to the linear coefficient ($7$).

Also, since all coefficients are positive, we only need to consider the *positive* factor pairs of $6$.

The positive factor pairs of $6$ are

$$
(1,6),\quad (2,3)
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(1,6)$ add to $7{:}$

$$
1+6 =7 \quad{\color{green}\checkmark}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $y+6y$, and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2y^{2} + 7y + 3 = \\
2y^{2} + y + 6y + 3 &=  \\
(2y^{2} + y) + (6y + 3) &=  \\
y(2y + 1) + 3(2y + 1) &=  \\
&= (y + 3)(2y + 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the original trinomial factors as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
6y^{2} + 21y + 9 &=  \\
3(2y^{2} + 7y + 3) &=  \\
&= 3(y + 3)(2y + 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

And we're done!

Whenever the coefficient of the quadratic term is negative, we should always factor this out first. $$

$$

$$
f'(x)\approx \frac{f(x) - f(x-h) }{h}
$$

This expression is known as the **backward difference approximation** because if $h>0$ then $x-h$ is a step behind $x$ (i.e., to the left).

17592186093445 :tutorial/content "Where does the formula for the backward difference come from? Remember that from the definition of derivative, we have the forward difference formula

$$
f'(x)\approx \frac{f(x+h) - f(x) }{h}
$$

for small values of  $h.$ 

Now, replacing $h$ with $-h$ in the formula above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & \approx \frac{f(x-h)-f(x)}{-h} \\  & =\frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

The step of replacing $h$ with $-h$ is equivalent to stepping a distance of $h$ to the left rather than to the right." :tutorial/id #uuid "1cc2d207-71d4-53a4-8c67-5af0c5f4d173" :tutorial/math-academy-id 371 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the Formula"} :step/id #uuid "a635f38c-a7e9-57d1-aeb5-e9fe6f8751e0" :step/math-academy-id 694}] :activity/title "Estimating Derivatives Using a Backward Difference Quotient" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186092467} {:db/id 17592186093335 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093444 :tutorial/content "To approximate the derivative of a function, we can use the finite difference formula

for small values of  $h.$ 

Now, replacing $h$ with $-h$ in the formula above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & \approx \frac{f(x-h)-f(x)}{-h} \\  & =\frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

The step of replacing $h$ with $-h$ is equivalent to stepping a distance of $h$ to the left rather than to the right." :tutorial/id #uuid "1cc2d207-71d4-53a4-8c67-5af0c5f4d173" :tutorial/math-academy-id 371 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the Formula"} {:course/id #uuid "992cac0c-bf6a-5373-95c9-02edfcfb591e" :course/math-academy-id 105 :db/id 17592186046644} {:db/id 17592186049506 :topic/difficulty 1.1081057366958396 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428973 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. $$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}) & =0 \\ 2x+\frac{2y}{4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ \frac{y}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{4x}{y}\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows that the parabola has its vertex at $O,$ and passes through the point $(-3,-1).$

The general equation of a left- or right-opening parabola whose vertex is at $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
{y}^{2}=4px.
$$

Substituting $x=-3$ and $y=-1$ into the equation above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)^{2} & =4p(-3) \\ 1 & =-12p \\ p & =-\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of our parabola is 

$$
{y}^{2}=-\frac{1}{3}x.
$$

Finally, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\frac{1}{3}x) \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{6y}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186317218 :question/id #uuid "a43aa514-b6a3-516e-bf25-cd1e713491f7" :question/math-academy-id "q-342218"} {:db/id 17592186317243 :question/id #uuid "Consider the circle below. How do we calculate $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ the slope of the tangent to this circle at any point on the circle? 

![](images/4c/4cfdf4a02935f6a729b12a81a5b48d0356e37046fb5dabfdeefc498a68b8ed8d.png)

To calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}$, we start by writing down the equation of the circle. Then, we differentiate the equation of the circle with respect to $x.$

Since our circle is centered at the origin and has a radius of $\sqrt{5},$ its equation is given by

$$
x^2 + y^2 = (\sqrt{5})^2 
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x^2 + y^2 = 5.
$$

Now, to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x},$ we differentiate the equation of the circle using implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the slope at any point on the circle using our expression for the derivative. 

For example, since the point $P\big( \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3} \big)$ satisfies the equation $x^2 + y^2 = 5,$ it must lie on the circle. Therefore, the slope of the tangent at this point is given by

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \Bigg|_{( \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3})} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{3}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "69315ade-3415-5abd-94e7-90d616fb7002" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5865 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6af5a081-1dac-5c00-aecb-60e48eb5a180" :step/math-academy-id \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the slope at any point on the circle using our expression for the derivative. 

For example, since the point $P\big( \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3} \big)$ satisfies the equation $x^2 + y^2 = 5,$ it must lie on the circle. Therefore, the slope of the tangent at this point is given by

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \Bigg|_{( \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3})} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{3}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "69315ade-3415-5abd-94e7-90d616fb7002" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5865 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6af5a081-1dac-5c00-aecb-60e48eb5a180" :step/math-academy-id 35885 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167751}} {:db/id 17592186168125 :tutorial/content "Consider the circle below. 17592186111702 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111825 :tutorial/content "Suppose we wish to plot the graph of $y=2^x$. First, we create a table of values:

| $x$ | $-3$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $y = 2^x$ | $\dfrac18$ | $\dfrac14$ | $\dfrac12$ | $1$ | $2$ | $4$ | $8$ |

Now, we can plot the graph:

![](images/e9/e987a8647092c836bde4bcea31dc075e80e9da36a67133fc2b9431b99c5e42ed.png)

Note the following key points:

1. The graph has a $y$-intercept at $(0,1)$.
2. The graph is increasing.
3. For $x>0$, the graph grows very rapidly as $x$ increases. Symbolically, we write $y\rightarrow \infty$ as $x\rightarrow \infty$.
4. For $x<0$, the graph gets very close to zero as $x$ decreases. However, it never actually reaches zero, so the graph has the horizontal asymptote $y=0$. Symbolically, we write $y\rightarrow 0$ as $x\rightarrow -\infty$.
5. The domain is $x\in (-\infty, \infty)$, and the range is $y>0$.

These key points apply to *any* exponential curve $y=a^x$ with $a>1$. These graphs always have the same general shape:

![](images/48/48f7bc7bb25bf1955d1e2cf48cffbf09e17f80a1228cada1c31f7ad4822bdace.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "1a4d886d-d7b8-5667-b52a-2c2eb4a35b91" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1540 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "af86e00c-f654-5321-9355-dbe234a657e3" :step/math-academy-id 516446 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111703}} {:db/id 17592186111703 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110732 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110310 :question/id #uuid "99ab6141-164f-5f36-b55b-6e7fa1c8770c" :question/math-academy-id "e-1215"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cf40e17e-0461-54a3-8f23-8424d694f189" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049619}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111145} {:db/id 17592186111335}] :knowledge-point/title "Sketching the Graph of an Exponential Growth Function"} :step/id #uuid "9c436809-f5cb-527a-907e-bd891aa0951c" :step/math-academy-id 516447 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111704}} {:db/id 17592186111704 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110733 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110311 :question/id #uuid "45473f44-206e-5eb6-a663-04d264e6a890" :question/math-academy-id "e-1216"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f6fa9e7b-172d-57b6-8b6e-0db0f8f802ad" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050255} {:db/id 17592186050580}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111223} {:db/id 17592186111334}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements about Exponential Growth Functions"} :step/id #uuid "de707c0a-c932-5251-81f5-798ae37e792e" :step/math-academy-id 516450 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111705}} {:db/id 17592186111705 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111826 :tutorial/content "Multiplying an exponential growth function by a positive number **scales** the graph in the vertical direction.

For example, the curve $y=2(3^x)$ represents a vertical scaling of $y=3^x$ by a factor of $2$. It takes all of the $y$-coordinates on $y=3^x$ and multiplies them by $2$. This has the effect of **stretching** the curve upwards.

![](images/49/49c2136298e6fbf1adcc4c24ddef6d3daf47367d4d3f15dc18c476dff086087a.png)

Notice that the horizontal asymptote at $y=0$ remained the same, and the $y$-intercept moved from $(0,1)$ to $(0,2)$.

In general, for *any* vertically stretched exponential curve $y=k(a^x)$,

- the horizontal asymptote at $y=0$ remains the same, and
- the $y$-intercept moves from $(0,1)$ to $(0,k)$." :tutorial/id #uuid "8c1fa510-e5f3-585b-852a-c46724144ec1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1541 :tutorial/title "Vertical Stretching"} :step/id #uuid "82779645-e04b-59c6-a05e-c042063885a7" :step/math-academy-id 516453 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111706}} {:db/id 17592186111706 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110734 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110369 :question/id #uuid "e5680653-d529-58df-b243-7447db0a750a" :question/math-academy-id "e-1802"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c7654997-ee9a-5d6c-88e9-d46f36bd8e88" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111098} {:db/id 17592186111387} {:db/id 17592186111399}] :knowledge-point/title "Plotting a Vertically Stretched Exponential Growth Function"} :step/id #uuid "4b8c5352-dd55-52e0-83dd-102169a1a723" :step/math-academy-id 516454 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111707}} {:db/id 17592186111707 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111833 :tutorial/content "The curve

$$
y=\dfrac{1}{3}(3^x)

represents a vertical scaling of $y=3^x$ by a factor of

$$
\dfrac{1}{3}

It takes all of the $y$-coordinates on $y=3^x$ and multiplies them by

Notice that the horizontal asymptote at $y=0$ remained the same, and the $y$-intercept moved from $(0,1)$ to

$$
\left(0,\dfrac{1}{3} \right)
$$

In general for *any* vertically stretched exponential curve $y=k(a^x)$,

- the horizontal asymptote at $y=0$ remains the same, and
- the $y$-intercept moves from $(0,1)$ to $(0,k)$." :tutorial/id #uuid "78c17e05-8ef3-58fd-a9ea-a2fc04f4bd83" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1858 :tutorial/title "Vertical Compression"} :step/id #uuid "254e2522-a3c6-57f8-9ac1-0e813acdc6d7" :step/math-academy-id 516458 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111708}} {:db/id 17592186111708 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110735 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110312 :question/id #uuid "3661675e-e7da-5834-97cf-017e4e084275" :question/math-academy-id "e-1217"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f8a6ac29-44ee-5305-be7a-41f9ae742756" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186110930} {:db/id 17592186111100}] :knowledge-point/title "Plotting a Vertically Compressed Exponential Growth Function"} :step/id #uuid "fbd6d68b-40b3-5cb7-afa4-487f4a8e9f03" :step/math-academy-id 516459}] :activity/title "Graphing Exponential Growth Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186110875} {:db/id 17592186111702 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111825 :tutorial/content "Suppose we wish to plot the graph of $y=2^x$. 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}+3y=f(x),\,y(0)=-1
$$

where $f(x)$ is a $2$-periodic function. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(0)=0.$*

The solution is 

$y(x)∼$  
{{field-1}} 
$+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=f(x)$ is given by

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},
$$

where ${y}_{c}$ is the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we find the homogeneous solution. The general solution of ${y}^{′}+3y=0$ is 

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-3x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

Next, we identify the form of the general solution. Because the operator ${y}^{′}+3y$ involves a first derivative, a periodic forcing function $f(x)$ results in a particular solution containing both sine and cosine terms:

$$
y(x)∼A{e}^{-3x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))
$$

Now, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=-1.$ Using the hint that the particular solution part evaluates to zero at $x=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A{e}^{-3(0)}+{y}_{p}(0) \\ -1 & =A(1)+0 \\ A & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $A$ back into the homogeneous part:

$$
{y}_{c}=-{e}^{-3x}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼-{e}^{-3x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365936 :question/id #uuid "0bafe4c7-5c26-53ec-8fd3-af5a2bac498d" :question/math-academy-id "q-343732" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186231418 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "742531ae-be2d-5fc8-8ef8-4f745c93bacd" :knowledge-point/title "Solving First-Order IVPs Using Fourier Series"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "91505a79-2ea5-54d7-95d8-90e5cea46420" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5{e}^{4x}" :db/id 17592186365938}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "91505a79-2ea5-54d7-95d8-90e5cea46420" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5{e}^{4x}" :db/id 17592186365938} :answer-field/id #uuid "fa3102c8-b53d-52e0-8f47-cacae0ffde3c" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186365937}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the initial value problem

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "$$
{y}^{″}+2{\pi }^{2}y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0
$$

Consider the initial value problem above, where $f(x)$ is an odd, $6$-periodic function. Select the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the second infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution of the differential equation.

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{18(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{3}(18-{n}^{2})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(x)$ is given by $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},$ where ${y}_{c}$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we address the particular solution ${y}_{p}.$ Since $f(x)$ is an odd function, its Fourier series consists only of sine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function. This is represented by the term

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{18(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{3}(18-{n}^{2})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Next, we find the homogeneous solution. The characteristic equation ${\lambda }^{2}+2{\pi }^{2}=0$ gives roots $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{2}\pi \text{i}.$ So, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\pi x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Using $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+0+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ because the particular solution is a sine series.

Next, we use the derivative condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0.$ First, we compute the derivative of the total solution (with $A=0$):

$$
{y}^{′}(x)∼B\sqrt{2}\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\pi x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(18-{n}^{2})}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Applying ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ and noting that $\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1,$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =B\sqrt{2}\pi +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(18-{n}^{2})} \\ B\sqrt{2}\pi  & =-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(18-{n}^{2})} \\ B & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(18-{n}^{2})} \\  & =-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{\sqrt{2}{\pi }^{3}(18-{n}^{2})} \\  & =-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3\sqrt{2}(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{3}(18-{n}^{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $B$ back into ${y}_{c}=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\pi x)$, we find the missing part:

$$
y(x)∼-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\pi x){\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3\sqrt{2}(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{3}(18-{n}^{2})}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{18(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{3}(18-{n}^{2})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365948 :question/id #uuid "e72e085b-8209-5b57-8832-a5f8ba9155db" :question/math-academy-id "q-343980"} {:db/id 17592186365954 :question/id #uuid 1020.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186231810} :activity/id #uuid "60204b9d-c0a9-5524-bd30-c8accd8e6729" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049479 :topic/id #uuid "f868b857-f4b2-5b40-8da2-046b9db36a57" :topic/math-academy-id 6721} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186231810 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231984 :tutorial/content "We know how to find a Fourier-series particular solution $y_p$ for a periodically forced linear ODE.
In this topic, the new step is how to use $y_p$ to satisfy an initial condition.

Recall that once a particular solution $y_p$ is chosen, the full solution has the form

$$
y = y_c + y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ solves the corresponding homogeneous equation.

Now, suppose the IVP is given at $x=x_0{:}$

$$
y(x_0)=y_0.
$$

Then,

$$
y_0 = y_c(x_0)+y_p(x_0).
$$

A useful simplification is to choose the particular solution so that

$$
y_p(x_0)=0.
$$

In that case, the initial condition becomes

$$
y_0 = y_c(x_0),
$$

so we can solve for the constant(s) in $y_c$ immediately (without evaluating any Fourier sums at $x_0$).

On the next slide, we’ll apply this idea in an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "4a6bfce3-0ee4-5ea7-905f-461e3f15500e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14713 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1d2d573d-acda-5605-a740-470ab9c3110a" :step/math-academy-id 607581 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231811}} {:db/id 17592186231811 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231993 :tutorial/content "For example, consider the initial value problem

$$
y'-2y = f(x), \qquad y(0)=3,
$$

where $f(x)$ is a $2$-periodic function. Suppose we choose the forcing (and hence the Fourier-series particular solution) so that

$$
y_p(0)=0.
$$

First, solve the homogeneous equation:

$$
y' - 2y = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y_c = Ae^{2x}.
$$

A $2$-periodic forcing function can be written using harmonics of frequency $\pi$, so we may write the particular solution in the form

$$
y_p(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n\cos(n\pi x)+b_n\sin(n\pi x)\right).
$$

Thus the full solution is

$$
y(x)=Ae^{2x}+\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n\cos(n\pi x)+b_n\sin(n\pi x)\right).
$$

Now apply $y(0)=3$ and use $y_p(0)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A{e}^{2(0)}+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 3 & =A(1)+0 \\ A & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
y(x)=
3e^{2x}+\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n\cos(n\pi x)+b_n\sin(n\pi x)\right).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ae6c43bc-e554-5975-9433-c7d67c2adbdd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14804 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "48c86314-12fc-57dd-bb24-3dab5839b9c1" :step/math-academy-id 607582 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231812}} {:db/id 17592186231812 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231418 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186231291 :question/id #uuid "b7a81b9e-d12c-55c7-b755-8f4e5b8115c7" :question/math-academy-id "e-21859"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "742531ae-be2d-5fc8-8ef8-4f745c93bacd" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049288}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186231565} {:db/id 17592186231566} {:db/id 17592186365933} {:db/id 17592186365936} {:db/id 17592186365939} {:db/id 17592186365942} {:db/id 17592186365945} {:db/id 17592186455449}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving First-Order IVPs Using Fourier Series"} :step/id #uuid "26e21ed5-3121-54a7-8a6b-1264c940acaa" :step/math-academy-id 607583 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231813}} {:db/id 17592186231813 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231989 :tutorial/content "When we solve a second-order IVP using Fourier series, we still represent the solution in the form

$$
y = y_c + y_p,
$$

but since the homogeneous solution has *two* constants, we use *two* conditions:

$$
y(0)=y_0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(0)=y_1
$$

Before we start, we can use the forcing series properties to simplify our work. For a second-order equation of the form 

$$
y'' + \omega^2 y = f(x)
$$

with no $y'$ (damping) term, the particular solution can be simplified. Here, we have two cases:

- **Case 1:** $f(x)$ is odd.

If $f(x)$ is *odd* and the equation has the form $y''+\omega^2 y=f(x)$, then the particular solution is also *odd*, so it is a sine series:

$$
y_p(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)
$$

This immediately gives $y_p(0)=0,$ so the condition $y(0)=y_0$ determines the cosine constant in $y_c$ without evaluating any infinite sum at $0$.

- **Case 2:** $f(x)$ is even.

If $f(x)$ is *even* and the equation has the form $y''+\omega^2 y=f(x)$, then the particular solution is also *even*, so it is a cosine series:

$$
y_p(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)
$$

Here, the derivative is a sine series:

$$
y_p'(x)=-\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{a_n n\pi}{L} \sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)
$$

This immediately gives $y_p'(0)=0,$ so the condition $y'(0)=y_1$ determines the sine constant in $y_c$ without evaluating any infinite sum at $0$.

In both cases, the key idea is that evaluating at $x=0$ (and differentiating once) lets the initial conditions pick off the constants in $y_c$ as cleanly as possible.

Let's see how this works in practice on the next slide." :tutorial/id #uuid "c8c0ab68-168a-57f1-9ab6-13bd9d042d32" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14781 :tutorial/title "Second-Order IVPs"} :step/id #uuid "ffe83dea-ed44-5451-a483-e07ad7977f77" :step/math-academy-id 607586 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231814}} {:db/id 17592186231814 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231990 :tutorial/content "Consider the initial value problem

$$
y''+ 7y = f(x), \qquad y(0)=3,\quad y'(0)=0
$$

where $f(x)$ is an even, $2\pi$-periodic function. Since the forcing is even and the differential operator contains no $y'$ term, we represent the particular solution as a cosine series:

$$
y_p(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos(nx)
$$

Next, we solve the homogeneous equation $y''+7y=0.$ The characteristic equation is $\lambda^2+7=0,$ so

$$
y_c=A\cos(\sqrt{7}x)+B\sin(\sqrt{7}x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Differentiating the total solution gives

$$
y'(x)=-A\sqrt{7}\sin(\sqrt{7}x)+B\sqrt{7}\cos(\sqrt{7}x)-\sum_{n=1}^\infty n a_n\sin(nx).
$$

Using the derivative condition $y'(0)=0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =-A\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+B\sqrt{7}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }n{a}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\ 0 & =0+B\sqrt{7}-0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because the total solution is an even function, its derivative is an odd function, which must vanish at $x=0.$

Next, we apply $y(0)=3.$ With $B=0,$ the total solution is

$$
y(x)\sim A\cos(\sqrt{7}x)+\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos(nx).
$$

Applying $y(0)=3$ and noting that $\cos(0)=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =A+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n} \\ A & =3-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution can be written as

$$
y(x)\sim 
\cos(\sqrt{7}x)\left(3-\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\right)
+\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos(nx).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "edbe311b-6f4f-5c28-96fa-394b23f30390" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14782 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example of a Second-Order IVP"} :step/id #uuid "3b6f9bb1-ddc0-5924-bda7-a089e2b187ec" :step/math-academy-id 607587 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231815}} {:db/id 17592186231815 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231419 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186231293 :question/id #uuid "97290d74-457b-522d-991d-7891e5a01d28" :question/math-academy-id "e-21876"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "81f5380b-7a7d-52c5-a530-3768e7cf3143" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186231568} {:db/id 17592186231569} {:db/id 17592186365927} {:db/id 17592186365948} {:db/id 17592186365954} {:db/id 17592186365960} {:db/id 17592186455480} {:db/id 17592186455496}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving Second-Order IVPs Using Fourier Series"} :step/id #uuid "3a843d13-ef46-5939-817d-692b8c15b4c0" :step/math-academy-id 607588}] :activity/title "Solving IVPs Using Fourier Series" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186231521} {:db/id 17592186231810 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231984 :tutorial/content "We know how to find a Fourier-series particular solution $y_p$ for a periodically forced linear ODE.

y' - 2y = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y_c = Ae^{2x}.
$$

A $2$-periodic forcing function can be written using harmonics of frequency $\pi$, so we may write the particular solution in the form

$$
y_p(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n\cos(n\pi x)+b_n\sin(n\pi x)\right).
$$

Thus the full solution is

$$
y(x)=Ae^{2x}+\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n\cos(n\pi x)+b_n\sin(n\pi x)\right).
$$

Now apply $y(0)=3$ and use $y_p(0)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A{e}^{2(0)}+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 3 & =A(1)+0 \\ A & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
y(x)=
3e^{2x}+\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n\cos(n\pi x)+b_n\sin(n\pi x)\right).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ae6c43bc-e554-5975-9433-c7d67c2adbdd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14804 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} {:db/id 17592186231812 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231418 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186231291 :question/id #uuid "b7a81b9e-d12c-55c7-b755-8f4e5b8115c7" :question/math-academy-id "e-21859"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "742531ae-be2d-5fc8-8ef8-4f745c93bacd" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049288}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186231565} {:db/id 17592186231566} {:db/id 17592186365933} {:db/id 17592186365936} {:db/id 17592186365939} {:db/id 17592186365942} {:db/id 17592186365945} {:db/id 17592186455449}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving First-Order IVPs Using Fourier Series"} :step/id #uuid "26e21ed5-3121-54a7-8a6b-1264c940acaa" :step/math-academy-id 607583 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231813}} {:db/id 17592186231813 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231989 :tutorial/content "When we solve a second-order IVP using Fourier series, we still represent the solution in the form

$$
y = y_c + y_p,
$$

but since the homogeneous solution has *two* constants, we use *two* conditions:

$$
y(0)=y_0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(0)=y_1
$$

Before we start, we can use the forcing series properties to simplify our work. For a second-order equation of the form 

$$
y'' + \omega^2 y = f(x)
$$

with no $y'$ (damping) term, the particular solution can be simplified. Here, we have two cases:

- **Case 1:** $f(x)$ is odd.

If $f(x)$ is *odd* and the equation has the form $y''+\omega^2 y=f(x)$, then the particular solution is also *odd*, so it is a sine series:

$$
y_p(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)
$$

This immediately gives $y_p(0)=0,$ so the condition $y(0)=y_0$ determines the cosine constant in $y_c$ without evaluating any infinite sum at $0$.

- **Case 2:** $f(x)$ is even.

If $f(x)$ is *even* and the equation has the form $y''+\omega^2 y=f(x)$, then the particular solution is also *even*, so it is a cosine series:

$$
y_p(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)
$$

Here, the derivative is a sine series:

$$
y_p'(x)=-\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{a_n n\pi}{L} \sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)
$$

This immediately gives $y_p'(0)=0,$ so the condition $y'(0)=y_1$ determines the sine constant in $y_c$ without evaluating any infinite sum at $0$.

In both cases, the key idea is that evaluating at $x=0$ (and differentiating once) lets the initial conditions pick off the constants in $y_c$ as cleanly as possible.

Let's see how this works in practice on the next slide." :tutorial/id #uuid "c8c0ab68-168a-57f1-9ab6-13bd9d042d32" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14781 :tutorial/title "Second-Order IVPs"} :step/id #uuid "ffe83dea-ed44-5451-a483-e07ad7977f77" :step/math-academy-id 607586 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231814}} {:db/id 17592186231989 :tutorial/content "When we solve a second-order IVP using Fourier series, we still represent the solution in the form

$$
y''+ 7y = f(x), \qquad y(0)=3,\quad y'(0)=0
$$

where $f(x)$ is an even, $2\pi$-periodic function. Since the forcing is even and the differential operator contains no $y'$ term, we represent the particular solution as a cosine series:

$$
y_p(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos(nx)
$$

Next, we solve the homogeneous equation $y''+7y=0.$ The characteristic equation is $\lambda^2+7=0,$ so

$$
y_c=A\cos(\sqrt{7}x)+B\sin(\sqrt{7}x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Differentiating the total solution gives

$$
y'(x)=-A\sqrt{7}\sin(\sqrt{7}x)+B\sqrt{7}\cos(\sqrt{7}x)-\sum_{n=1}^\infty n a_n\sin(nx).
$$

Using the derivative condition $y'(0)=0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =-A\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+B\sqrt{7}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }n{a}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\ 0 & =0+B\sqrt{7}-0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because the total solution is an even function, its derivative is an odd function, which must vanish at $x=0.$

Next, we apply $y(0)=3.$ With $B=0,$ the total solution is

$$
y(x)\sim A\cos(\sqrt{7}x)+\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos(nx).
$$

Applying $y(0)=3$ and noting that $\cos(0)=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =A+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n} \\ A & =3-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution can be written as

$$
y(x)\sim 
\cos(\sqrt{7}x)\left(3-\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\right)
+\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos(nx).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "edbe311b-6f4f-5c28-96fa-394b23f30390" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14782 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example of a Second-Order IVP"} :step/id #uuid "3b6f9bb1-ddc0-5924-bda7-a089e2b187ec" :step/math-academy-id 607587 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231815}} {:db/id 17592186231990 :tutorial/content "Consider the initial value problem

:question/problem "Given the hyperboloid of two sheets $(x-1)^2 + y^2 - \dfrac{z^2}{4} = -1,$ find the domain of $z = z(x,y).$" :question/worked-solution "From the hyperboloid equation, we make $z$ the subject as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{4} & =-1 \\ (x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2}+1 & =\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{z}^{2}}{4} & =(x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2}+1 \\ {z}^{2} & =4((x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2}+1) \\ z & =\pm 2\sqrt{(x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

The square root is defined only for non-negative arguments. However, notice that for all $(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2,$ we have

$$
(x-1)^2 + y^2 + 1 \geq 0.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+(y-1)^{2}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+(y-1)^{2}-1 & =\frac{{z}^{2}}{16}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2} & =16(\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+(y-1)^{2}-1) \\ z & =\pm 4\sqrt{\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+(y-1)^{2}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+(y-1)^{2}-1 & \ge 0 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+(y-1)^{2} & \ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the exterior of the ellipse $\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+(y-1)^{2}=1,$ which includes the boundary.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{(x-5)^{2}}{8}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{50}+(z-3)^{2} & =-1 \\ -\frac{(x-5)^{2}}{8}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{50}+1=-1 \\ -\frac{(x-5)^{2}}{8}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{50} & =-2 \\ \frac{(x-5)^{2}}{8}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{50} & =2 \\ \frac{(x-5)^{2}}{16}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{100} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-5)^{2}}{{4}^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{10}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/id #uuid "a715d0ff-c3bf-59f0-8f15-f8770c11ebac" :topic/math-academy-id 1892} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125375 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125773 :tutorial/content "A **hyperboloid of one sheet** centered at $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ is a quadric surface whose equation is given by

$$\dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} - \dfrac{(z-z_0)^2}{c^2} =1,$$

where $a,$ $b,$ and $c$ are constants.

For example, the graph of the hyperboloid of one sheet

$$x^2+y^2-z^2=1$$

is shown below. It has its center at the origin, and the $z$-axis is the **axis of symmetry** of the hyperboloid.

![](images/0d/0d97e5ac26685b49bcdb3155866bd34ba83bd758f02035b500d3f594fc5716c8.png)

The intercepts of this hyperboloid with the coordinate axes are as follows:

- the $x$-intercepts are $(\pm1,0,0)$
- the $y$-intercepts are $(0,\pm1,0)$
- there are no $z$-intercepts" :tutorial/id #uuid "b15b84bd-ab8f-5ade-8289-c1795374ab94" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3438 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9b1de06e-be8c-5534-9c53-59e61058ffb5" :step/math-academy-id 19457 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125379}} {:db/id 17592186125376 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124503 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124312 :question/id #uuid "e85cfe0b-4ff6-5cce-9384-aeb930843b49" :question/math-academy-id "e-5265"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b079a5ff-e73a-592f-b16c-8740682538f3" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050992}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124825} {:db/id 17592186124988} {:db/id 17592186284467} {:db/id 17592186284468} {:db/id 17592186284469} {:db/id 17592186323801} {:db/id 17592186339004} {:db/id 17592186342131} {:db/id 17592186378920} {:db/id 17592186408095} {:db/id 17592186408096} {:db/id 17592186488228}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Domain of a Hyperboloid"} :step/id #uuid "4ba1a392-70de-526a-ac89-008dd6fbf4e5" :step/math-academy-id 19458 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125459}} {:db/id 17592186125379 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125775 :tutorial/content "A **hyperboloid of two sheets** centered at $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ is given by

$$\dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} - \dfrac{(z-z_0)^2}{c^2} =-1.$$

**Watch out!** This equation is similar to the general equation of a hyperboloid of one sheet. The only difference is the right-hand side is now $-1$ instead of $+1.$

For example, the graph of the hyperboloid of two sheets

$$x^2+y^2-z^2=-1$$

is represented below. It has its center at the origin, and the $z$-axis is the **axis of symmetry** of the hyperboloid.

![](images/96/96ec4196c3e299d2e57cdb8a3a2a06094452bf05e2f66e43fc60c059077b305f.png)

The intercepts of this hyperboloid with the $z$-axis are $(0,0,\pm1).$ The surface does not intersect the $x$- or $y$-axes.

Calculating the intercepts of a hyperboloid with the coordinate axes is done in the same way as we've seen before with spheres and ellipsoids. Let's see some examples.

There is a simple way to distinguish between hyperboloids of one and two sheets by simply looking at the equations:

- *one* minus sign indicates hyperboloids of *one* sheet: $$\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2} \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}-} \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}=1$$
- *two* minus signs indicate hyperboloids of *two* sheets: $$\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2} \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}-} \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}= \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}-}1$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d9a4fb57-50db-54d3-a354-5c56c44b5b3b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3440 :tutorial/title "Hyperboloids of Two Sheets"} :step/id #uuid "4ed11bf9-ec94-5810-9687-5899a45bf9cc" :step/math-academy-id 19462 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125634}} {:db/id 17592186125458 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124555 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124364 :question/id #uuid "1fbe37ed-9022-5c44-851c-0e66fe2fb79f" :question/math-academy-id "e-6078"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d28eda1a-a90b-57e9-969a-eb36552e413e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048866} {:db/id 17592186049699}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124881} {:db/id 17592186124882} {:db/id 17592186284476} {:db/id 17592186284478} {:db/id 17592186284479} {:db/id 17592186339024} {:db/id 17592186339027} {:db/id 17592186378934} {:db/id 17592186380008} {:db/id 17592186380015} {:db/id 17592186380022} {:db/id 17592186391951} {:db/id 17592186488263}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Traces of Hyperboloids"} :step/id #uuid "fb6a05b0-ef9d-5743-a9b2-a3a300f5e53f" :step/math-academy-id 22380} {:db/id 17592186125459 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125804 :tutorial/content "So far, we've encountered hyperboloids whose axes of symmetry are parallel to the $z$-axis. 
Let's now consider the cases when a hyperboloid is oriented along the $x$- or the $y$-axes.

For a hyperboloid of one sheet centered at the origin, the other two cases are as follows:

- When the $y$ term is negative, the axis of symmetry is the $y$-axis.

$$
\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} + \frac{z^2}{c^2} =1
$$

![](images/85/854a4e7506aa8e14fd19ceaadb5311a2d83596d27b33224272c41fa0639ea996.png)

- When the $x$ term is negative, the axis of symmetry is the $x$-axis.

$$
-\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} + \frac{z^2}{c^2} =1
$$

![](images/ef/effc9d579d8d2ba00fec421fb1800639ccb4fba440e4518a5454d4ca282bc2d3.png)

Likewise, for a hyperboloid of two sheets centered at the origin, the other two cases are as follows:

- When the $y$ term is negative, the axis of symmetry is the $y$-axis.

$$
\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} + \frac{z^2}{c^2} =-1
$$

![](images/2b/2b77432e38466d0983c196aed51eecd614096d971f21b0c68804e71a39548210.png)

- When the $x$ term is negative, the axis of symmetry is the $x$-axis.

$$
-\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} + \frac{z^2}{c^2} =-1
$$

![](images/4d/4d3b7e21da4acb5c13320c248c9cbe220488f43cfcbe328ad0416b22f449d143.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "37ea72a1-3f48-5ba4-94e5-ad5a2e962723" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3850 :tutorial/title "Alternative Orientations of the Axis of Symmetry"} :step/id #uuid "2deb75ff-8eff-541a-bff6-4a30ea363312" :step/math-academy-id 22397 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125635}} {:db/id 17592186125634 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124650 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124213 :question/id #uuid "58966f53-5f83-5c86-8ffe-38ad0dffd2b3" :question/math-academy-id "e-12555"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cf44a846-8458-5e2f-bef3-72cf87a6035f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049477} {:db/id 17592186051028}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124826} {:db/id 17592186124827} {:db/id 17592186124883} {:db/id 17592186284462} {:db/id 17592186284463} {:db/id 17592186284466} {:db/id 17592186323679} {:db/id 17592186378906} {:db/id 17592186380001} {:db/id 17592186401453}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Intercepts of a Hyperboloid"} :step/id #uuid "55a21c7e-3632-5bac-88a2-92a6bd3c409d" :step/math-academy-id 45274 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125637}} {:db/id 17592186125635 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125877 :tutorial/content "The traces of a hyperboloid of one sheet are either ellipses or hyperbolas.

For example, let's find the traces with the coordinate planes for the hyperboloid of one sheet given by

$$
x^2+y^2-z^2=1.
$$

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{0}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a circle centered at the origin of radius $1$ in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/b3/b369958a609ba3861be5d32fbf3195b6feb241228f81e89bb116b29f80e38318.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a hyperbola in the $xz$-plane centered at the origin.

![](images/4c/4c77b8758877ac88a73dece8c52f3b9cb650c4176edad5db020b138d70e0393b.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a hyperbola in the $yz$-plane centered at the origin.

![](images/0d/0ddcfc2e78166fa801a46deccd30c4cc2ddc12e81ae2e81508b5e13a374c208f.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "f3dfcfe4-330c-5142-8314-d09baa6e8acf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7836 :tutorial/title "Traces of Hyperboloids of One Sheet"} :step/id #uuid "f7656072-e089-540b-89c4-8df18945b7f8" :step/math-academy-id 45276 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125636}} {:db/id 17592186125636 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125878 :tutorial/content "The traces of a hyperboloid of two sheets are either ellipses, hyperbolas, a single point, or the empty set.

For example, let's find the traces with the coordinate planes for the hyperboloid of two sheets given by

$$
x^2+y^2-z^2=-1.
$$

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is the empty set since the surface does not intersect the $xy$-plane.

![](images/96/96ec4196c3e299d2e57cdb8a3a2a06094452bf05e2f66e43fc60c059077b305f.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-1 \\ {x}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a hyperbola in the $xz$-plane centered at the origin.

![](images/71/71d280f0b887b4805c882362dab8c9b13ef08b83f91904bce487ef749a67a6ab.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-1 \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a hyperbola in the $yz$-plane centered at the origin.

![](images/34/3425d7f8df3a4dbbb5fa5763baf499e220215d0e33a0914859b8d1707074145d.png)

There are a few other cases we should note:

- The trace of our surface with the plane $z=1$ is a single point (the vertex of the upper sheet):

$$
x^2+y^2 - 1^2 = -1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (x,y,z) = (0,0,1)
$$

Likewise, the trace of our surface with the plane $z=-1$ is another point (the vertex of the lower sheet):

$$
x^2+y^2 - (-1)^2 = -1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (x,y,z) = (0,0,-1)
$$

- The trace of our surface with the horizontal plane $z=k$ for $|k| > 1$ is a circle:

$$
x^2+y^2 - k^2 = -1 \quad\Longrightarrow x^2+y^2 = k^2-1
$$

![](images/0c/0c91656e9656d4958de2b82f24ae05a6611d24d1cf0536384fbdd873d2e10e1d.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "16cf67e7-24e7-5523-991e-af37acd35e60" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7837 :tutorial/title "Traces of Hyperboloids of Two Sheets"} :step/id #uuid "3e256a50-c4bf-5ba0-8f3e-b65f84c0fe2c" :step/math-academy-id 45277 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125458}} {:db/id 17592186125637 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125879 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the graphs a typical one-sheet and two-sheet hyperboloids centered at $O,$ as shown below.

![](images/45/45359d1c73d9cdc721068dbee0e27bedb8cde622bae0615c16862e4157b2baf3.png)

Notice that a hyperboloid of two sheets is defined for any $(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ In fact, for any point $(x,y)$ in the $xy$-plane, there are exactly two points on the hyperboloid. 

On the other hand, the graph of a hyperboloid of one sheet does not contain points over the central elliptical region (close to the axis of symmetry).

For example, given the hyperboloid of one sheet $x^2 + y^2 - z^2 = 1,$ let's find the domain of $z = z(x,y).$

From the hyperboloid equation, we make $z$ the subject as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1 & ={z}^{2} \\ {z}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1 \\ z & =\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the square root is defined only for non-negative arguments, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1 & \ge 0 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & \ge 1,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the *exterior* and boundary of the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1.$

Therefore, the domain of $z(x,y)$ for the hyperboloid $x^2+y^2-z^2 = 1$ is

$$
\left \{(x,y) \: : \: x^2 + y^2 \geq 1 \right\}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4d2a84b4-9a16-51d5-a343-bc7826406b8e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7838 :tutorial/title "The Domain of a Hyperboloid"} :step/id #uuid "203c24cd-0b43-5e99-91fc-7f9c44b7b75c" :step/math-academy-id 45281 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125376}}] :activity/title "Hyperboloids" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124695} {:db/id 17592186125375 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125773 :tutorial/content "A **hyperboloid of one sheet** centered at $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ is a quadric surface whose equation is given by

$$\dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} - \dfrac{(z-z_0)^2}{c^2} =1,$$

where $a,$ $b,$ and $c$ are constants.

For example, the graph of the hyperboloid of one sheet

$$x^2+y^2-z^2=1$$

is shown below. It has its center at the origin, and the $z$-axis is the **axis of symmetry** of the hyperboloid.

![](images/0d/0d97e5ac26685b49bcdb3155866bd34ba83bd758f02035b500d3f594fc5716c8.png)

The intercepts of this hyperboloid with the coordinate axes are as follows:

- the $x$-intercepts are $(\pm1,0,0)$
- the $y$-intercepts are $(0,\pm1,0)$
- there are no $z$-intercepts" :tutorial/id #uuid "b15b84bd-ab8f-5ade-8289-c1795374ab94" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3438 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9b1de06e-be8c-5534-9c53-59e61058ffb5" :step/math-academy-id 19457 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125379}} {:db/id 17592186125773 :tutorial/content "A **hyperboloid of one sheet** centered at $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ is a quadric surface whose equation is given by

$$\dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} - \dfrac{(z-z_0)^2}{c^2} =1,$$

where $a,$ $b,$ and $c$ are constants.

For example, the graph of the hyperboloid of one sheet

$$x^2+y^2-z^2=1$$

is shown below. It has its center at the origin, and the $z$-axis is the **axis of symmetry** of the hyperboloid.

![](images/0d/0d97e5ac26685b49bcdb3155866bd34ba83bd758f02035b500d3f594fc5716c8.png)

The intercepts of this hyperboloid with the coordinate axes are as follows:

- the $x$-intercepts are $(\pm1,0,0)$
- the $y$-intercepts are $(0,\pm1,0)$
- there are no $z$-intercepts" :tutorial/id #uuid "b15b84bd-ab8f-5ade-8289-c1795374ab94" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3438 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186125379 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125775 :tutorial/content "A **hyperboloid of two sheets** centered at $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ is given by

$$\dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} - \dfrac{(z-z_0)^2}{c^2} =-1.$$

**Watch out!** This equation is similar to the general equation of a hyperboloid of one sheet. The only difference is the right-hand side is now $-1$ instead of $+1.$

For example, the graph of the hyperboloid of two sheets

$$x^2+y^2-z^2=-1$$

is represented below. It has its center at the origin, and the $z$-axis is the **axis of symmetry** of the hyperboloid.

The intercepts of this hyperboloid with the $z$-axis are $(0,0,\pm1).$ The surface does not intersect the $x$- or $y$-axes.

Calculating the intercepts of a hyperboloid with the coordinate axes is done in the same way as we've seen before with spheres and ellipsoids. Let's see some examples.

There is a simple way to distinguish between hyperboloids of one and two sheets by simply looking at the equations:

- *one* minus sign indicates hyperboloids of *one* sheet: $$\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2} \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}-} \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}=1$$

- When the $x$ term is negative, the axis of symmetry is the $x$-axis.

- When the $x$ term is negative, the axis of symmetry is the $x$-axis.

$$

![](images/4d/4d3b7e21da4acb5c13320c248c9cbe220488f43cfcbe328ad0416b22f449d143.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "37ea72a1-3f48-5ba4-94e5-ad5a2e962723" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3850 :tutorial/title "Alternative Orientations of the Axis of Symmetry"} {:db/id 17592186125635 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125877 :tutorial/content "The traces of a hyperboloid of one sheet are either ellipses or hyperbolas.

For example, let's find the traces with the coordinate planes for the hyperboloid of one sheet given by

$$
x^2+y^2-z^2=1.
$$

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{0}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a circle centered at the origin of radius $1$ in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/b3/b369958a609ba3861be5d32fbf3195b6feb241228f81e89bb116b29f80e38318.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a hyperbola in the $xz$-plane centered at the origin.

![](images/4c/4c77b8758877ac88a73dece8c52f3b9cb650c4176edad5db020b138d70e0393b.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a hyperbola in the $yz$-plane centered at the origin.

![](images/0d/0ddcfc2e78166fa801a46deccd30c4cc2ddc12e81ae2e81508b5e13a374c208f.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "f3dfcfe4-330c-5142-8314-d09baa6e8acf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7836 :tutorial/title "Traces of Hyperboloids of One Sheet"} :step/id #uuid "f7656072-e089-540b-89c4-8df18945b7f8" :step/math-academy-id 45276 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125636}} {:db/id 17592186125637 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125879 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the graphs a typical one-sheet and two-sheet hyperboloids centered at $O,$ as shown below.

![](images/45/45359d1c73d9cdc721068dbee0e27bedb8cde622bae0615c16862e4157b2baf3.png)

Notice that a hyperboloid of two sheets is defined for any $(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ In fact, for any point $(x,y)$ in the $xy$-plane, there are exactly two points on the hyperboloid. 

On the other hand, the graph of a hyperboloid of one sheet does not contain points over the central elliptical region (close to the axis of symmetry).

For example, given the hyperboloid of one sheet $x^2 + y^2 - z^2 = 1,$ let's find the domain of $z = z(x,y).$

From the hyperboloid equation, we make $z$ the subject as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1 & ={z}^{2} \\ {z}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1 \\ z & =\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the square root is defined only for non-negative arguments, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1 & \ge 0 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & \ge 1,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the *exterior* and boundary of the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1.$

Therefore, the domain of $z(x,y)$ for the hyperboloid $x^2+y^2-z^2 = 1$ is

$$
\left \{(x,y) \: : \: x^2 + y^2 \geq 1 \right\}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4d2a84b4-9a16-51d5-a343-bc7826406b8e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7838 :tutorial/title "The Domain of a Hyperboloid"} :step/id #uuid "203c24cd-0b43-5e99-91fc-7f9c44b7b75c" :step/math-academy-id 45281 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125376}} {:db/id 17592186125877 :tutorial/content "The traces of a hyperboloid of one sheet are either ellipses or hyperbolas.

For example, let's find the traces with the coordinate planes for the hyperboloid of one sheet given by

$$
x^2+y^2-z^2=1.
$$

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{0}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a circle centered at the origin of radius $1$ in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/b3/b369958a609ba3861be5d32fbf3195b6feb241228f81e89bb116b29f80e38318.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a hyperbola in the $xz$-plane centered at the origin.

![](images/4c/4c77b8758877ac88a73dece8c52f3b9cb650c4176edad5db020b138d70e0393b.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a hyperbola in the $yz$-plane centered at the origin.

![](images/0d/0ddcfc2e78166fa801a46deccd30c4cc2ddc12e81ae2e81508b5e13a374c208f.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "f3dfcfe4-330c-5142-8314-d09baa6e8acf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7836 :tutorial/title "Traces of Hyperboloids of One Sheet"} {:db/id 17592186125636 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125878 :tutorial/content "The traces of a hyperboloid of two sheets are either ellipses, hyperbolas, a single point, or the empty set.

For example, let's find the traces with the coordinate planes for the hyperboloid of two sheets given by

$$
x^2+y^2-z^2=-1.
$$

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is the empty set since the surface does not intersect the $xy$-plane.

![](images/96/96ec4196c3e299d2e57cdb8a3a2a06094452bf05e2f66e43fc60c059077b305f.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-1 \\ {x}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a hyperbola in the $xz$-plane centered at the origin.

![](images/71/71d280f0b887b4805c882362dab8c9b13ef08b83f91904bce487ef749a67a6ab.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-1 \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a hyperbola in the $yz$-plane centered at the origin.

![](images/34/3425d7f8df3a4dbbb5fa5763baf499e220215d0e33a0914859b8d1707074145d.png)

There are a few other cases we should note:

- The trace of our surface with the plane $z=1$ is a single point (the vertex of the upper sheet):

$$
x^2+y^2 - 1^2 = -1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (x,y,z) = (0,0,1)
$$

Likewise, the trace of our surface with the plane $z=-1$ is another point (the vertex of the lower sheet):

$$
x^2+y^2 - (-1)^2 = -1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (x,y,z) = (0,0,-1)
$$

- The trace of our surface with the horizontal plane $z=k$ for $|k| > 1$ is a circle:

$$
x^2+y^2 - k^2 = -1 \quad\Longrightarrow x^2+y^2 = k^2-1
$$

![](images/0c/0c91656e9656d4958de2b82f24ae05a6611d24d1cf0536384fbdd873d2e10e1d.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "16cf67e7-24e7-5523-991e-af37acd35e60" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7837 :tutorial/title "Traces of Hyperboloids of Two Sheets"} :step/id #uuid "3e256a50-c4bf-5ba0-8f3e-b65f84c0fe2c" :step/math-academy-id 45277 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125458}} {:db/id 17592186125878 :tutorial/content "The traces of a hyperboloid of two sheets are either ellipses, hyperbolas, a single point, or the empty set.

For example, let's find the traces with the coordinate planes for the hyperboloid of two sheets given by

$$

$$

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is the empty set since the surface does not intersect the $xy$-plane.

![](images/96/96ec4196c3e299d2e57cdb8a3a2a06094452bf05e2f66e43fc60c059077b305f.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-1 \\ {x}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a hyperbola in the $xz$-plane centered at the origin.

![](images/71/71d280f0b887b4805c882362dab8c9b13ef08b83f91904bce487ef749a67a6ab.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-1 \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-1,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a hyperbola in the $yz$-plane centered at the origin.

![](images/34/3425d7f8df3a4dbbb5fa5763baf499e220215d0e33a0914859b8d1707074145d.png)

There are a few other cases we should note:

- The trace of our surface with the plane $z=1$ is a single point (the vertex of the upper sheet):

$$
x^2+y^2 - 1^2 = -1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (x,y,z) = (0,0,1)
$$

Likewise, the trace of our surface with the plane $z=-1$ is another point (the vertex of the lower sheet):

$$
x^2+y^2 - (-1)^2 = -1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (x,y,z) = (0,0,-1)
$$

- The trace of our surface with the horizontal plane $z=k$ for $|k| > 1$ is a circle:

$$
x^2+y^2 - k^2 = -1 \quad\Longrightarrow x^2+y^2 = k^2-1
$$

![](images/0c/0c91656e9656d4958de2b82f24ae05a6611d24d1cf0536384fbdd873d2e10e1d.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "16cf67e7-24e7-5523-991e-af37acd35e60" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7837 :tutorial/title "Traces of Hyperboloids of Two Sheets"} {:db/id 17592186125879 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the graphs a typical one-sheet and two-sheet hyperboloids centered at $O,$ as shown below.

![](images/45/45359d1c73d9cdc721068dbee0e27bedb8cde622bae0615c16862e4157b2baf3.png)

Notice that a hyperboloid of two sheets is defined for any $(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ In fact, for any point $(x,y)$ in the $xy$-plane, there are exactly two points on the hyperboloid. 

On the other hand, the graph of a hyperboloid of one sheet does not contain points over the central elliptical region (close to the axis of symmetry).

For example, given the hyperboloid of one sheet $x^2 + y^2 - z^2 = 1,$ let's find the domain of $z = z(x,y).$

From the hyperboloid equation, we make $z$ the subject as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1 & ={z}^{2} \\ {z}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1 \\ z & =\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the square root is defined only for non-negative arguments, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1 & \ge 0 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & \ge 1,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the *exterior* and boundary of the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1.$

Therefore, the domain of $z(x,y)$ for the hyperboloid $x^2+y^2-z^2 = 1$ is

$$
\left \{(x,y) \: : \: x^2 + y^2 \geq 1 \right\}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4d2a84b4-9a16-51d5-a343-bc7826406b8e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7838 :tutorial/title "The Domain of a Hyperboloid"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046659} $$

which gives the exterior of the ellipse $\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+(y-1)^{2}=1,$ which includes the boundary.

$$

find the domain of $z=z(x,y).$" :question/worked-solution "From the hyperboloid equation, we make $z$ the subject as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2}-(z-3)^{2} & =1 \\ (x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2}-1 & =(z-3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(z-3)^{2} & =(x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2}-1 \\ z-3 & =\pm \sqrt{(x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} \\ z & =3\pm \sqrt{(x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the square root is defined only for non-negative arguments, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2}-1 & \ge 0 \\ (x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2} & \ge 1,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the exterior of the circle $(x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ which includes the boundary.

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\,:\,(x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2}\ge 1\}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "346ce6bc-5f2c-5170-a37c-8daa10ff6d75" :step/next {:db/id 17592186488342}} {:db/id 17592186488333 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284468 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "051774ba-959a-5c1e-a9f4-ba2f7128c841" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}^{2}" :db/id 17592186281733} {:answer/id #uuid "3dcc081f-8c87-52c8-b3e1-e3a8a332e58f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}\le 1\}" :db/id 17592186487686} {:answer/id #uuid "a77b95d1-fceb-5a52-bb2a-611c7c686bdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}<1\}" :db/id 17592186487882} {:answer/id #uuid "d3c48da9-56f6-56f4-b48e-a9ee4cfebf84" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}>1\}" :db/id 17592186487969} {:answer/id #uuid "e4f233b9-83c6-5d23-a7ab-9cd273335e98" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}\ge 1\}" :db/id 17592186488003}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186281733} :answer-field/id #uuid "f0ed39c8-50b3-5c43-b5b6-cec23b5c61a4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284360}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5e42866d-b20f-5a25-a416-745497c6d775" :question/math-academy-id "q-164305" :question/problem "Given the hyperboloid of two sheets ${x}^{2}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}-{z}^{2}=-1,$ find the domain of $z=z(x,y).$" :question/worked-solution "From the hyperboloid equation, we make $z$ the subject as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}-{z}^{2} & =-1 \\ {x}^{2}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}+1 & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}+1 \\ z & =\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

The square root is defined only for non-negative arguments. However, notice that for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2},$ we have

$$
{x}^{2}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}+1\ge 0.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}-{z}^{2} & =-1 \\ {x}^{2}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}+1 & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}+1 \\ z & =\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

The square root is defined only for non-negative arguments. However, notice that for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2},$ we have

$$
{x}^{2}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}+1\ge 0.
$$

$$
