multiplication principles.

First, we apply the addition principle, subtracting $4$ from both sides:

$$
\eqalign{
    		2x+4{\color{red}\:-\:4} &=10{\color{red}\:-\:4}\
               2x+0&=6\
		2x &=6
	}
$$

Second, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\require{cancel}
	\eqalign{
    		\dfrac{2x}{\color{red}2} &=\dfrac{6}{\color{red}2}\
                \dfrac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{\color{red}2}} &= 3 \
		x &=3
	}
$$

So $x=3$ is our solution. Let's plug this back into the original equation, to be sure that it's correct.

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+4 & =10 \\ 2\cdot 3+4 & =10 \\ 6+4 & =10 \\ 10 & =10\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** When solving these types of equations, we always apply the addition principle first, and the multiplication principle second." :tutorial/id #uuid "f8f52cdf-9de7-5b27-addc-4bc35612fa15" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8055 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "362ed182-60db-5089-b1e6-79bd2e6be30b" :step/math-academy-id 175799 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055603}} {:db/id 17592186055603 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054654 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054384 :question/id #uuid "8955a3ce-a161-5dc5-8ec0-c357a0403b46" :question/math-academy-id "e-12862"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b170bf27-76bc-5558-9133-e81a4760072f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048725} {:db/id 17592186050613}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186054941} {:db/id 17592186055056} {:db/id 17592186055227} {:db/id 17592186486391} {:db/id 17592186486411} {:db/id 17592186503722}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving Linear Equations that Involve Multiplication"} :step/id #uuid "80f9fb5b-00db-570c-a6f4-98191654603b" :step/math-academy-id 175800 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055604}} {:db/id 17592186055604 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054655 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054385 :question/id #uuid "074b5213-4f4e-5d1b-a5c4-8b5403901b4d" :question/math-academy-id "e-12863"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "52c2b31a-9b7a-52cb-9fa7-111de8bc53ea" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055057} {:db/id 17592186055058} {:db/id 17592186055059} {:db/id 17592186055279} {:db/id 17592186486386} {:db/id 17592186486417}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving Linear Equations while Keeping the Variable on the Right-Hand Side"} :step/id #uuid "14f3a665-daa8-52a3-ae20-e94b27c5c513" :step/math-academy-id 175804 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055605}} {:db/id 17592186055605 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056013 :tutorial/content "Solving equations with both the addition and multiplication principles can be a lot of work. There are often many steps to write down. However, we don't have to write down all of the steps.

For example, when using the multiplication principle to solve

$$
\dfrac{y}{2} = 5,
$$

the set of full steps are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{2} & =5 \\ 2\cdot \frac{y}{2} & =2\cdot 5 \\ \frac{2y}{2} & =10 \\ \frac{\cancel{2}y}{\cancel{2}} & =10 \\ y & =10\end{aligned}
$$

However, if we cancel out the $2$'s to indicate that they disappear, then we can skip writing down several of the steps.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{2} & =5 \\ \cancel{2}\cdot \frac{y}{\cancel{2}} & =2\cdot 5 \\ y & =10\end{aligned}

![](images/46/46a85010d46969ffb7df440efd72bb3fa8d1394b35cc2887ee4567cda15079c5.png)

The sum of the length of its sides is called the **perimeter**. Here, the perimeter of our triangle is

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =AB+BC+AC \\  & =2+4.2+3.8 \\  & =10\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7664d7c3-e47c-57b6-97aa-1131f036852c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2244 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "2dd79ef0-aa4a-5d52-ba67-92d8d47fd909" :step/math-academy-id 623181 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106738}} {:db/id 17592186106738 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105806 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105528 :question/id #uuid "00942425-ab13-5a50-a63a-d29cf2f34889" :question/math-academy-id "e-2752"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b1d4b0c2-10d0-5c3a-8a58-4d7598dd9f96" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049027} {:db/id 17592186050410}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106137} {:db/id 17592186106384} {:db/id 17592186492074}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Perimeter of a Triangle Given the Perimeter of Another Triangle"} :step/id #uuid "48b5c886-bff4-52b2-b702-6be7c990ade1" :step/math-academy-id 623182 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106739}} {:db/id 17592186106739 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107045 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a quadrilateral $ABCD$ as shown below and it is known that ${AD} = 6\,\mathrm{m},$ ${AB} = 2\,\mathrm{m},$ ${BC} = 4\,\mathrm{m},$ and $CD=5\,\mathrm{m}.$ What is the perimeter of the quadrilateral?   

![](images/a7/a74251f1c72eccad42b98e0d3fd9a7e7cd0a60018a6f03bb65ec2abc34eb1c88.png)

Remember that the **perimeter** $p$ of a polygon is the sum of the measures of all its sides. So, we can simply calculate 

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =AD+AB+BC+CD \\  & =6+2+4+5 \\  & =17\,m.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0428807f-e6a6-5280-81bc-ab454203aebf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2246 :tutorial/title "Perimeters of Polygons"} :step/id #uuid "2154c4c2-efe1-5888-87e0-905e612555d4" :step/math-academy-id 623185 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106740}} {:db/id 17592186106740 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105807 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105529 :question/id #uuid "b4864184-6983-58ab-9787-524e04dc5c73" :question/math-academy-id "e-2754"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6f6c0ca1-297a-5f25-bccf-c74d0c565c24" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106202} {:db/id 17592186106203} {:db/id 17592186492033} {:db/id 17592186492041}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Perimeter of a Polygon"} :step/id #uuid "2896eab9-aca7-5163-8e08-2101c4fa2827" :step/math-academy-id 623186 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106741}} {:db/id 17592186106741 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107046 :tutorial/content "Let's take a look at the polygons depicted below and find their perimeters.

From the picture, we conclude that polygons I, II and III all have a perimeter of $10$ while polygon IV has a perimeter of $8.$

Some examples of regular polygons are shown below.

![](images/d3/d33f23d3d3e301e336d7f70f37e88eee0f605c31b098969805d7c6346e34470e.png)

Some examples of polygons that are **NOT** regular are as follows:

- The rectangle below is **NOT** regular since the sides are not all congruent.

![](images/6d/6d0c6eaee1ae1932d3bd44013c0b8aca977cbe0d98242d5c10aaa24d4f281a77.png)

- The rhombus below is **NOT** regular since the interior angles are not all congruent.

![](images/ce/ce2b908945db56934f08dc0da47f6c708f5220bce3a80f5147362c8b915c5613.png)

- A $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle is **NOT** regular since neither the sides nor the angles are all congruent.

![](images/bf/bfe00eb1d1374252fd12f6c74eff7c052021a7305ce10027efc8869f561e3ef5.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "cd59495c-0fc7-5db8-8d91-05d02fa8e26f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7926 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f6dcb244-ba60-524d-bafc-0fd7ed3097aa" :step/math-academy-id 119188 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106554}} {:db/id 17592186106554 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105696 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105470 :question/id #uuid "fbeb62a5-1a2c-53df-ab8d-6aaee87c4a11" :question/math-academy-id "e-12647"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e9f78a76-4d2f-5694-971c-e734bc330602" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049584} {:db/id 17592186050164}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106075} {:db/id 17592186106076} {:db/id 17592186507464} {:db/id 17592186507524}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Regular Polygons"} :step/id #uuid "91bb4d37-5646-5ecb-b152-184d3a1e7df5" :step/math-academy-id 119189 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106555}} {:db/id 17592186106555 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107160 :tutorial/content "![](images/24/24c4c952103f245cd4dc32e34d5dd2363478f5400ddecfbe2503130135c01946.png)

Consider the regular pentagon above. What is the measure of each interior angle?

Recall that the sum of the interior angles of a polygon with $n$ sides equals $180^\circ \cdot (n-2).$ 

All interior angles in a regular polygon are congruent. So, to calculate the measure of each interior angle, we find the sum of the interior angles and divide by the number of angles.

A pentagon has $n=5$ sides. Therefore, the sum of its interior angles is

$$
180^\circ \times (5 - 2) = 540^\circ.
$$

 

Therefore, the measure of each interior angle is

$$
\dfrac{540^\circ}{5} = 108^\circ,
$$

as shown below.

Consider the regular hexagon above. What is the measure of each *exterior* angle?

Note the following:

- The exterior angles in a regular polygon are all congruent.

$$
\dfrac{360^\circ}{6} = 60^\circ,
$$

Consider the regular hexagon above. What is the measure of each *exterior* angle?

Note the following:

- The exterior angles in a regular polygon are all congruent.

- The sum of the exterior angles of *any* convex polygon equals $360^\circ.$

So, to find the measure of the exterior angles of a regular polygon, we divide $360^\circ$ by the number of sides.

Since a regular hexagon has $n=6$ sides, the measure of each exterior angle is

$$
\dfrac{360^\circ}{6} = 60^\circ,
$$

as shown below.

Therefore, the polygons are congruent, and we can write

lamina about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "The moment of a lamina $D$ with the mass density function $\lambda (x,y)$ about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{M}_{y}={∬}_{D}x\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, $D$ is represented as a type II plane region and $\lambda (x,y)=5xy.$ 

Therefore, the moment is

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}x\cdot 5xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}5{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3y}5{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}5y{\int }_{0}^{3y}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}5y{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=3y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}5y(9{y}^{3}-0)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}45{y}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[9{y}^{5}]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281613 :question/id #uuid "13f35429-2bb3-5bdd-9f21-f76be76ab433" :question/math-academy-id "q-163152"} {:db/id 17592186281615 :question/id #uuid $$
{M}_{x}={∬}_{D}y\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}y\cdot \frac{1}{xy}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{y}}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}[\operatorname{ln}⁡x]_{x=1}^{x={e}^{y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=1}^{y=3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(9-1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}

4166} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186199256 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199454 :tutorial/content "Recall that a lamina's *center of mass* is the point $(\overline{x}, \overline{y})$ where its total mass could be concentrated to give the same total moment about the coordinate axes as the original lamina. 

The center of mass of a lamina $D$ with the mass density function $\lambda(x,y)$ is given by 

$$
(\overline{x},\overline{y}) = \left( \dfrac{M_y}{m}, \dfrac{M_x}{m} \right),
$$

where 

- $\displaystyle m = \iint \limits_D \lambda (x,y) \: \textrm{d}A$ is the mass of the lamina,

- $\displaystyle M_x = \iint\limits_D y \, \lambda (x,y) \: \textrm{d}A\:$ is the moment of the lamina about the $x$-axis, and

- $\displaystyle M_y = \iint\limits_D x \, \lambda (x,y) \: \textrm{d}A$ is the moment of the lamina about the $y$-axis.

Remember that if we could place a fulcrum under our lamina at its center of mass, it would balance perfectly." :tutorial/id #uuid "dbc92201-9cb2-54d6-9ac9-8ee49bf8c4e5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4905 :tutorial/title "Center of Mass"} :step/id #uuid "274308ee-bab4-54df-9e77-953f260e7982" :step/math-academy-id 30624 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199258}} {:db/id 17592186199257 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199455 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to determine the center of mass of a thin lamina whose mass is unevenly distributed. 

We describe the mass distribution across a lamina using its mass density function $\lambda (x,y).$ This function tells us the *mass per unit area* at any point $(x,y)$ on the lamina.

For example, consider a thin plate with mass density function $\lambda(x,y) = 6xy$ occupying the finite rectangular region $D$ between the lines $x=1,$ $x=2,$ $y=0,$ and $y=1.$ What is the moment of the plate about the $y$-axis?

To answer this, consider a point $(x,y) \in D$ on the plate and a small rectangular piece with its bottom-left corner at $(x,y)$ and area $\Delta{A},$ as shown below.

![](images/8c/8cd947e542aaf7eb787abc7a846e87a2d03ccafa0987f3422928fdcba115da9e.png)

If $\Delta{A}$ is very small, we can assume that our density function is approximately constant over the selected piece. As a result, the moment of this piece about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{M}_{y} & ≈x\cdot Δm \\  & ≈x\cdot 6xy\,ΔA \\  & =6{x}^{2}y\,ΔA.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the total moment of the plate about the axis, we add together the moments of all such pieces and take the limit as $\Delta{A} \to 0.$ By doing this, we get

$$
M_y =  \iint\limits_D 6x^2y \: \textrm{d}A.
$$

 

Carrying out the integration, we find that the moment of the plate about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}6{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}6{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,\text{d}y \\  & =[{x}^{3}]_{x=1}^{x=2}\cdot [{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =(8-1)\cdot (1-0) \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

The moment about the $x$-axis can be found similarly.

In general, the moments $M_x$ and $M_y$ of a lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda(x,y)$ about the $x$-axis and about the $y$-axis, respectively, are given by the following formulas:

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}y\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\ {M}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}x\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7aa18cfe-acd7-5e17-982c-58eabc063404" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4906 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "751210ed-66b0-57b2-8130-be9ebe7e72a9" :step/math-academy-id 30625 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199330}} {:db/id 17592186199258 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198364 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198238 :question/id #uuid "8199670b-efe4-537b-8f8a-228d567a0944" :question/math-academy-id "e-8182"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3f7a06a8-0260-5b59-b3a5-c02ee03980d4" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198962} {:db/id 17592186198975} {:db/id 17592186235552} {:db/id 17592186281619} {:db/id 17592186281620} {:db/id 17592186281664} {:db/id 17592186281665} {:db/id 17592186281666} {:db/id 17592186419225} {:db/id 17592186419230} {:db/id 17592186419232} {:db/id 17592186419236} {:db/id 17592186419237}] :knowledge-point/title "Find the Center of Mass of a Plane Lamina"} :step/id #uuid "d8381e14-c44b-5f31-9e2d-03ef40423eb9" :step/math-academy-id 30626 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199259}} {:db/id 17592186199259 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199456 :tutorial/content "When a lamina's mass density is constant, the center of mass depends only on the shape of the lamina. In cases like these, the center of mass is called the **centroid** of the lamina. The centroid of a shape corresponds to its geometrical center.

So, $\lambda$ is constant, then the mass of the plate is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={∬}_{D}\lambda \,dA \\  & =\lambda {∬}_{D}\,dA \\  & =\lambda \cdot {A}_{D},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A_D$ denotes the area of $D.$ As a result, 

$$
m = \lambda \cdot A_D \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \dfrac{\lambda}{m} = \dfrac{1}{A_D}.
$$

Substituting the above into the formula for the $x$-coordinate of the center of mass, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{M}_{y}}{m} & =\frac{1}{m}{∬}_{D}x\,\lambda \,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{\lambda }{m}{∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{{A}_{D}}{∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

We can similarly compute the $y$-coordinate.

In general, the centroid of a lamina $D$ with area $A_D$ is given by $(x_c, y_c),$ where

$$
\displaystyle x_c = \dfrac{1}{A_D} \iint\limits_D x \, \: \textrm{d}A, \qquad 
\displaystyle y_c = \dfrac{1}{A_D} \iint\limits_D y \, \: \textrm{d}A.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "aea964ff-901c-5b76-9fca-721d53f04354" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4907 :tutorial/title "Centroids"} :step/id #uuid "c6144c3d-16c1-5ac5-841d-01a96fe71c2e" :step/math-academy-id To find the total moment of the plate about the axis, we add together the moments of all such pieces and take the limit as $\Delta{A} \to 0.$ By doing this, we get

$$
M_y =  \iint\limits_D 6x^2y \: \textrm{d}A.
$$

 

Carrying out the integration, we find that the moment of the plate about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}6{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}6{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,\text{d}y \\  & =[{x}^{3}]_{x=1}^{x=2}\cdot [{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =(8-1)\cdot (1-0) \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

The moment about the $x$-axis can be found similarly.

In general, the moments $M_x$ and $M_y$ of a lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda(x,y)$ about the $x$-axis and about the $y$-axis, respectively, are given by the following formulas:

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}y\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\ {M}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}x\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7aa18cfe-acd7-5e17-982c-58eabc063404" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4906 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "751210ed-66b0-57b2-8130-be9ebe7e72a9" :step/math-academy-id 30625 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199330}} {:db/id 17592186199256 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199454 :tutorial/content "Recall that a lamina's *center of mass* is the point $(\overline{x}, \overline{y})$ where its total mass could be concentrated to give the same total moment about the coordinate axes as the original lamina. 

The center of mass of a lamina $D$ with the mass density function $\lambda(x,y)$ is given by 

$$
(\overline{x},\overline{y}) = \left( \dfrac{M_y}{m}, \dfrac{M_x}{m} \right),
$$

where 

- $\displaystyle m = \iint \limits_D \lambda (x,y) \: \textrm{d}A$ is the mass of the lamina,

- $\displaystyle M_x = \iint\limits_D y \, \lambda (x,y) \: \textrm{d}A\:$ is the moment of the lamina about the $x$-axis, and

- $\displaystyle M_y = \iint\limits_D x \, \lambda (x,y) \: \textrm{d}A$ is the moment of the lamina about the $y$-axis.

Remember that if we could place a fulcrum under our lamina at its center of mass, it would balance perfectly." :tutorial/id #uuid "dbc92201-9cb2-54d6-9ac9-8ee49bf8c4e5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4905 :tutorial/title "Center of Mass"} :step/id #uuid "274308ee-bab4-54df-9e77-953f260e7982" :step/math-academy-id 30624 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199258}} {:db/id 17592186199454 :tutorial/content "Recall that a lamina's *center of mass* is the point $(\overline{x}, \overline{y})$ where its total mass could be concentrated to give the same total moment about the coordinate axes as the original lamina. 

The center of mass of a lamina $D$ with the mass density function $\lambda(x,y)$ is given by

$$

where

We describe the mass distribution across a lamina using its mass density function $\lambda (x,y).$ This function tells us the *mass per unit area* at any point $(x,y)$ on the lamina.

For example, consider a thin plate with mass density function $\lambda(x,y) = 6xy$ occupying the finite rectangular region $D$ between the lines $x=1,$ $x=2,$ $y=0,$ and $y=1.$ What is the moment of the plate about the $y$-axis?

To answer this, consider a point $(x,y) \in D$ on the plate and a small rectangular piece with its bottom-left corner at $(x,y)$ and area $\Delta{A},$ as shown below.

![](images/8c/8cd947e542aaf7eb787abc7a846e87a2d03ccafa0987f3422928fdcba115da9e.png)

If $\Delta{A}$ is very small, we can assume that our density function is approximately constant over the selected piece. As a result, the moment of this piece about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{M}_{y} & ≈x\cdot Δm \\  & ≈x\cdot 6xy\,ΔA \\  & =6{x}^{2}y\,ΔA.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the total moment of the plate about the axis, we add together the moments of all such pieces and take the limit as $\Delta{A} \to 0.$ By doing this, we get

$$
M_y =  \iint\limits_D 6x^2y \: \textrm{d}A.
$$

 

Carrying out the integration, we find that the moment of the plate about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}6{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}6{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,\text{d}y \\  & =[{x}^{3}]_{x=1}^{x=2}\cdot [{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =(8-1)\cdot (1-0) \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

The moment about the $x$-axis can be found similarly.

In general, the moments $M_x$ and $M_y$ of a lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda(x,y)$ about the $x$-axis and about the $y$-axis, respectively, are given by the following formulas:

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}y\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\ {M}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}x\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7aa18cfe-acd7-5e17-982c-58eabc063404" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4906 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186199330 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198407 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198049 :question/id #uuid "9294903c-1b4c-58b6-a878-7f2220ec763d" :question/math-academy-id "e-12470"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "444e9b54-f6d4-5b70-af49-d01556bb3135" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049267} {:db/id 17592186049333} {:db/id 17592186050326} {:db/id 17592186050409}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198629} {:db/id 17592186198652} {:db/id 17592186235550} {:db/id 17592186281559} {:db/id 17592186281560} {:db/id 17592186281562} {:db/id 17592186281582} {:db/id 17592186419224} {:db/id 17592186419226} {:db/id 17592186419234} {:db/id 17592186419241}] :knowledge-point/title "The Moment of a Plane Lamina About the X-Axis"} :step/id #uuid "6a2f3763-0f5f-5328-a240-5a9328c979b3" :step/math-academy-id 44905 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199329}} {:db/id 17592186199259 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199456 :tutorial/content "When a lamina's mass density is constant, the center of mass depends only on the shape of the lamina. In cases like these, the center of mass is called the **centroid** of the lamina. The centroid of a shape corresponds to its geometrical center.

So, $\lambda$ is constant, then the mass of the plate is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={∬}_{D}\lambda \,dA \\  & =\lambda {∬}_{D}\,dA \\  & =\lambda \cdot {A}_{D},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A_D$ denotes the area of $D.$ As a result, 

$$
m = \lambda \cdot A_D \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \dfrac{\lambda}{m} = \dfrac{1}{A_D}.
$$

Substituting the above into the formula for the $x$-coordinate of the center of mass, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{M}_{y}}{m} & =\frac{1}{m}{∬}_{D}x\,\lambda \,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{\lambda }{m}{∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{{A}_{D}}{∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

We can similarly compute the $y$-coordinate.

In general, the centroid of a lamina $D$ with area $A_D$ is given by $(x_c, y_c),$ where

$$
\displaystyle x_c = \dfrac{1}{A_D} \iint\limits_D x \, \: \textrm{d}A, \qquad 
\displaystyle y_c = \dfrac{1}{A_D} \iint\limits_D y \, \: \textrm{d}A.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "aea964ff-901c-5b76-9fca-721d53f04354" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4907 :tutorial/title "Centroids"} :step/id #uuid "c6144c3d-16c1-5ac5-841d-01a96fe71c2e" :step/math-academy-id 30627 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199260}} {:db/id 17592186199456 :tutorial/content "When a lamina's mass density is constant, the center of mass depends only on the shape of the lamina. "809502b3-ee2f-5a96-8373-13e255b37eac" :topic/math-academy-id 263} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186060460 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060872 :tutorial/content "In isosceles right triangles such as the one shown below, the angles always measure $45^\circ,$ $45^\circ,$ and $90^\circ.$ 

Consequently, isosceles right triangles are often called **$\boldsymbol{45^\circ}$-$\boldsymbol{45^\circ}$-$\boldsymbol{90^\circ}$ triangles**.

![](images/d3/d32159528abc75f3ed8bcccaedb2765b676fd6cc64164e2f8c81f98eb37f6db4.png)

All $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangles share a special property:

*In any ${45^\circ}$-${45^\circ}$-${90^\circ}$ triangle, the length of the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg.*

To see why this is, remember that

- in an isosceles triangle, the two legs must have the same length, and

- in a right triangle, the square of the longest side must equal the sum of the squares of the two shorter sides.

So, if an isosceles right triangle has legs of length $a$ and the hypotenuse has length $h,$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{a}^{2} \\ {h}^{2} & =2{a}^{2} \\ h & =\sqrt{2{a}^{2}} \\ h & =\sqrt{2}\cdot a.\end{aligned}

Consequently, isosceles right triangles are often called **$\boldsymbol{45^\circ}$-$\boldsymbol{45^\circ}$-$\boldsymbol{90^\circ}$ triangles**.

![](images/d3/d32159528abc75f3ed8bcccaedb2765b676fd6cc64164e2f8c81f98eb37f6db4.png)

All $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangles share a special property:

*In any ${45^\circ}$-${45^\circ}$-${90^\circ}$ triangle, the length of the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg.*

To see why this is, remember that

- in an isosceles triangle, the two legs must have the same length, and

- in a right triangle, the square of the longest side must equal the sum of the squares of the two shorter sides.

So, if an isosceles right triangle has legs of length $a$ and the hypotenuse has length $h,$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{a}^{2} \\ {h}^{2} & =2{a}^{2} \\ h & =\sqrt{2{a}^{2}} \\ h & =\sqrt{2}\cdot a.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7e5fefd4-4ac4-5999-8c6d-0ad927da9ca6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2381 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "8b5ee65a-7747-5a0e-9d06-721118b74e10" :step/math-academy-id 10416 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060461}} {:db/id 17592186060872 :tutorial/content "In isosceles right triangles such as the one shown below, the angles always measure $45^\circ,$ $45^\circ,$ and $90^\circ.$

axis of symmetry of the elliptic paraboloid $z= 4x^2 + 8(y + 2)^2.$" :question/worked-solution "The general equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $z$-axis with vertex at a point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ is 

$$
z - z_0 = \dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2}.
$$

To find the vertex, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-0 & =4{x}^{2}+8(y+2)^{2} \\ z-0 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{1/4}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{1/8} \\ z-0 & =\frac{(x-0)^{2}}{1/4}+\frac{(y-(-2))^{2}}{1/8}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $z$-axis that has its vertex at $(0,-2,0).$  Since it is oriented along the $z$-axis, we conclude that its axis of symmetry is parallel to the $z$-axis.

The axis of symmetry should pass through the vertex of the paraboloid. Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry can be written as an intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=0 \\ y=-2\end{aligned}

:topic/math-academy-id 1893} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125377 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125774 :tutorial/content "Consider the quadric surface with the equation

$$z = x^2 + y^2$$

whose graph is shown below.

![](images/14/14e8d23a4bc649257c2f7351e0d2c1d62e39a8cd8eed1467e65853ee121b836e.png)

This surface is an example of an **elliptic paraboloid.**

The **vertex** of this elliptic paraboloid is located at the origin, and its **axis of symmetry** is the $z$-axis. Note that the axis of symmetry is the vertical line that passes through the vertex.

More generally, the equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $z$-axis whose vertex is at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ is given by

$$z - z_0 = \dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2},$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

These surfaces are called *elliptic* *paraboloids* because their traces in the $xy$-plane are *ellipses*, while their traces in the $yz$- and $xz$-planes are *parabolas*. We'll discuss the traces of this surface in more detail shortly." :tutorial/id #uuid "d5da7d20-bcec-546d-8cd6-178215fc2096" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3439 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0155d173-f619-5729-9721-6203bf768219" :step/math-academy-id 19459 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125378}} {:db/id 17592186125378 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124504 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124313 :question/id #uuid "945f684f-9707-5a0a-b5d7-0753f11b4385" :question/math-academy-id "e-5266"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ddf82ff9-ea7c-5f7f-ac18-07f8e75b717e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048350} {:db/id 17592186049336} {:db/id 17592186050991}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124896} {:db/id 17592186124931} {:db/id 17592186125218} {:db/id 17592186284456} {:db/id 17592186284457} {:db/id 17592186284458} {:db/id 17592186339072} {:db/id 17592186381300}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Properties of an Elliptic Paraboloid"} :step/id #uuid "32ea6077-6c22-5a3f-bce8-05b8b28c4283" :step/math-academy-id 19461 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125380}} {:db/id 17592186125380 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125776 :tutorial/content "Now consider the graph of the quadric surface

$$z = x^2 -y^2$$

whose graph is shown below.

![](images/5f/5f02c207742c737d00cdeabbd2cbba93a88a42521c41a2cc1e9f19d27ff55f20.png)

This surface is an example of a **hyperbolic paraboloid** whose **saddle point** is at the origin.

More generally, a hyperbolic paraboloid whose saddle point is at $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ has the general equation $$z - z_0 = \dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2}- \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2}$$

where $a$ and $b$ constants.

This surface is called *hyperbolic* *paraboloid* because its traces in the $xy$-plane are *hyperbolas*, while its traces in the $yz$- and $xz$-planes are *parabolas*. We'll discuss the traces of this surface in more detail shortly.

Another property is that this surface mirrors itself across the planes $x=0$ and $y=0.$ Since these planes meet along the $z$-axis, that axis serves as the **axis of symmetry** of the hyperbolic paraboloid." :tutorial/id #uuid "15370709-5e87-5dcb-8a1f-ff66b0bf86e0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3442 :tutorial/title "Hyperbolic Paraboloids"} :step/id #uuid "68121b3e-5396-564e-baa5-4f10972910c1" 17592186418046}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Traces of Paraboloids"} :step/id #uuid "d6a4a4b3-6632-5593-890e-334f7d6d897e" :step/math-academy-id 22414} {:db/id 17592186125461 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125805 :tutorial/content "So far, we've encountered elliptic paraboloids whose axes of symmetry are parallel to the $z$-axis. Let's now consider the cases when an elliptic paraboloid is oriented along the $x$- or the $y$-axes.

For an elliptic paraboloid, the other two cases are as follows.

- When the vertex is at the origin and the $y$ term is linear, the axis of symmetry is the $y$-axis: $$y = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}$$

![](images/da/da37415ddd27764a719fecc5780ee91e6e8ad3f5ce877101b81d1a955c57eb6f.png)
- When the vertex is at the origin and the $x$ term is linear, the axis of symmetry is the $x$-axis: $$x = \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}$$

![](images/d1/d1488d9f4767312795a84ce6441f64dd567223d1de4da66adbd6e39de9612a53.png)

Likewise, for a hyperbolic paraboloid, the other two cases are as follows:

- When the saddle point is at the origin and the $y$ term is linear, the axis of symmetry is the $y$-axis. The two corresponding equations are $$y = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad y = \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} - \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}.$$
- When the saddle point is at the origin and the $x$ term is linear, the axis of symmetry is the $x$-axis. The two corresponding equations are $$x = \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad x = \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} - \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}.$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7f53539f-e8db-5205-b9d0-3919805097ae" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3851 :tutorial/title "Alternative Orientations of the Axis of Symmetry"} :step/id #uuid "26ce593b-6eaa-5a9c-a0cc-f0cf3649224d" :step/math-academy-id 22415 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125638}} {:db/id 17592186125638 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125880 :tutorial/content "The traces of an elliptic paraboloid are either ellipses, parabolas, a single point, or the empty set.

For example, let's find the traces with the coordinate planes for the elliptic paraboloid given by

$$z=x^2+y^2.$$

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation $$\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =0,\end{aligned}$$ which corresponds to the origin $(0,0,0).$

![](images/02/021dd988863021f564a0e85fb3db93030740059f2a50ade6504b3e12a5665372.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation $$\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2} & =z \\ {x}^{2} & =z,\end{aligned}$$ which is a parabola in the $xz$-plane that has its vertex at the origin.

![](images/9f/9f6cd0703b5d7b2458cbfd688d91f08a79752fa1ccd3616e5975f5c017aa7b42.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation $$\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =z \\ {y}^{2} & =z,\end{aligned}$$ which is a parabola in the $yz$-plane that has its vertex at the origin.

![](images/89/89be283ed121d3e30b1913e4412b8d3556ed611ef2a9a9bfd686d0594409f5c9.png)

There are a few other cases we should note:

- The trace of our surface with the plane $z=-k$ for $k > 0$ is the empty set. This is because $z\geq 0$ everywhere on the elliptic paraboloid.
- The trace of our surface with the plane $z=k$ for $k > 0$ is an ellipse: $$x^2+y^2 = k$$

![](images/f1/f15e925431b0d2ccfd4afa703cad1bcb37b65a75e96fbeabcf4823703bf184e5.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "0ea2e49f-f5aa-57b1-9b67-de6947a0e6e5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7839 :tutorial/title "Traces of Elliptic Paraboloids"} :step/id #uuid "587634e3-d3a5-57e5-bd78-93b3ed921e5b" :step/math-academy-id 45282 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125639}} {:db/id 17592186125639 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125881 :tutorial/content "The traces of a hyperbolic paraboloid are either hyperbolas, parabolas, or intersecting lines.

For example, let's find the traces with the coordinate planes for the hyperbolic paraboloid given by

$$z=x^2-y^2.$$

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation $$\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =0 \\ {y}^{2} & ={x}^{2} \\ y & =\pm x\end{aligned}$$ which corresponds to two intersecting lines in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/9b/9b3fbb9d8945c5d9208a59d404e489e4a339082c602c18154010e3e53083b220.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation $$\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{0}^{2} & =z \\ z & ={x}^{2},\end{aligned}$$ which corresponds to the parabola in the $xz$-plane that has its vertex at the origin.

![](images/e8/e8e2b6306052e781fd149e4eebb04da79eddb44b5261b05b129f208ad523b70b.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation $$\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =z \\ z & =-{y}^{2},\end{aligned}$$ which corresponds to the parabola in the $yz$-plane that has its vertex at the origin.

![](images/70/7010e4c26af60c6c27f66c93b805a2bac1e191c1646b5aac3a77f5dd3dadc64f.png)

In this particular case, the **saddle point** is at the origin. It is a minimum point for the trace in the $xz$-plane but a maximum point for the trace in the $yz$-plane.

Finally, note that the trace of our surface with the plane $z=k\neq 0$ is a hyperbola: $$x^2-y^2 = k$$

The **vertex** of this elliptic paraboloid is located at the origin, and its **axis of symmetry** is the $z$-axis. Note that the axis of symmetry is the vertical line that passes through the vertex.

Let's now consider the cases when an elliptic paraboloid is oriented along the $x$- or the $y$-axes.

For an elliptic paraboloid, the other two cases are as follows.

- When the vertex is at the origin and the $y$ term is linear, the axis of symmetry is the $y$-axis: $$y = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}$$

![](images/da/da37415ddd27764a719fecc5780ee91e6e8ad3f5ce877101b81d1a955c57eb6f.png)
- When the vertex is at the origin and the $x$ term is linear, the axis of symmetry is the $x$-axis: $$x = \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}$$

![](images/d1/d1488d9f4767312795a84ce6441f64dd567223d1de4da66adbd6e39de9612a53.png)

Likewise, for a hyperbolic paraboloid, the other two cases are as follows:

- When the saddle point is at the origin and the $y$ term is linear, the axis of symmetry is the $y$-axis. The two corresponding equations are $$y = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad y = \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} - \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}.$$
- When the saddle point is at the origin and the $x$ term is linear, the axis of symmetry is the $x$-axis. The two corresponding equations are $$x = \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad x = \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} - \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}.$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7f53539f-e8db-5205-b9d0-3919805097ae" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3851 :tutorial/title "Alternative Orientations of the Axis of Symmetry"} :step/id #uuid "26ce593b-6eaa-5a9c-a0cc-f0cf3649224d" :step/math-academy-id 22415 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125638}} {:db/id 17592186125460 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124556 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124365 :question/id #uuid "5ce5b329-ac5d-5581-b396-eadd569b9bec" :question/math-academy-id "e-6087"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "dff86a8b-7966-53f7-a7bc-287990fb611d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049118} {:db/id 17592186049699}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124897} {:db/id 17592186124923} {:db/id 17592186284464} {:db/id 17592186284465} {:db/id 17592186323729} {:db/id 17592186323730} {:db/id 17592186381910} {:db/id 17592186381935} {:db/id 17592186402441} {:db/id 17592186402475} {:db/id 17592186418046}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Traces of Paraboloids"} :step/id #uuid "d6a4a4b3-6632-5593-890e-334f7d6d897e" :step/math-academy-id 22414} {:db/id 17592186125805 :tutorial/content "So far, we've encountered elliptic paraboloids whose axes of symmetry are parallel to the $z$-axis. Let's now consider the cases when an elliptic paraboloid is oriented along the $x$- or the $y$-axes.

For an elliptic paraboloid, the other two cases are as follows.

- When the vertex is at the origin and the $y$ term is linear, the axis of symmetry is the $y$-axis: $$y = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}$$

![](images/da/da37415ddd27764a719fecc5780ee91e6e8ad3f5ce877101b81d1a955c57eb6f.png)
- When the vertex is at the origin and the $x$ term is linear, the axis of symmetry is the $x$-axis: $$x = \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}$$

![](images/d1/d1488d9f4767312795a84ce6441f64dd567223d1de4da66adbd6e39de9612a53.png)

Likewise, for a hyperbolic paraboloid, the other two cases are as follows:

- When the saddle point is at the origin and the $y$ term is linear, the axis of symmetry is the $y$-axis. The two corresponding equations are $$y = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad y = \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} - \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}.$$
- When the saddle point is at the origin and the $x$ term is linear, the axis of symmetry is the $x$-axis. The two corresponding equations are $$x = \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad x = \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} - \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}.$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7f53539f-e8db-5205-b9d0-3919805097ae" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3851 :tutorial/title "Alternative Orientations of the Axis of Symmetry"} {:db/id 17592186125638 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125880 :tutorial/content "The traces of an elliptic paraboloid are either ellipses, parabolas, a single point, or the empty set.

For example, let's find the traces with the coordinate planes for the elliptic paraboloid given by

$$z=x^2+y^2.$$

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation $$\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =0,\end{aligned}$$ which corresponds to the origin $(0,0,0).$

![](images/02/021dd988863021f564a0e85fb3db93030740059f2a50ade6504b3e12a5665372.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation $$\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2} & =z \\ {x}^{2} & =z,\end{aligned}$$ which is a parabola in the $xz$-plane that has its vertex at the origin.

![](images/9f/9f6cd0703b5d7b2458cbfd688d91f08a79752fa1ccd3616e5975f5c017aa7b42.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation $$\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =z \\ {y}^{2} & =z,\end{aligned}$$ which is a parabola in the $yz$-plane that has its vertex at the origin.

![](images/89/89be283ed121d3e30b1913e4412b8d3556ed611ef2a9a9bfd686d0594409f5c9.png)

There are a few other cases we should note:

- The trace of our surface with the plane $z=-k$ for $k > 0$ is the empty set. This is because $z\geq 0$ everywhere on the elliptic paraboloid.
- The trace of our surface with the plane $z=k$ for $k > 0$ is an ellipse: $$x^2+y^2 = k$$

$z=4$  onto the $xy$-plane is an ellipse. What are the lengths of the semi-axes of the ellipse?" :question/worked-solution "To find the intersection of the paraboloid and the plane $z=4$, we substitute $z=4$ into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

$$

- $4z + 3 = 4z + 9$

- $2z - 5 = z + 1$

- $3z - 2 = 3z - 2$" :question/worked-solution "Let's attempt to solve each equation in turn:

- For the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4z+3 & =4z+9 \\ 4z+3-4z & =4z+9-4z \\ 3 & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is false for all values of $z.$ Therefore, the equation $4z + 3 = 4z + 9$ has no solutions.

- For the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2z-5 & =z+1 \\ 2z-5-z+5 & =z+1-z+5 \\ z & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $2z - 5 = z + 1$ has the unique solution $z = 6.$

- For the third equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3z-2 & =3z-2 \\ 3z-2-3z & =3z-2-3z \\ -2 & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is true for all values of $z.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186048213} {:db/id 17592186476177} {:db/id 17592186204600 :question/id #uuid "d5d365bc-e325-5d06-ae8b-3799791feb02" :question/math-academy-id :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Which of the following equations has no solutions?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $-3u+4=-3u-1$
- **II.** $2u+5=2u+8$
- **III.** $6u-2=3u+1$" :question/worked-solution "Let's attempt to solve each equation in turn:

- For the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-3u+4 & =-3u-1 \\ -3u+4+3u & =-3u-1+3u \\ 4 & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is false for all values of $u.$ Therefore, the equation $-3u+4=-3u-1$ has no solutions.

- For the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2u+5 & =2u+8 \\ 2u+5-2u & =2u+8-2u \\ 5 & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is false for all values of $u.$ Therefore, the equation $2u+5=2u+8$ has no solutions.

- For the third equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}6u-2 & =3u+1 \\ 6u-2-3u+2 & =3u+1-3u+2 \\ 3u & =3 \\ u & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $6u-2=3u+1$ has the unique solution $u=1.$

$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants, and $b\neq 0.$ If $a = 0,$ then the equation has no solution.

First, we rewrite the equation in the form $ax = b.$ 

We start by adding $4x$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2nx+7 & =-4x+5 \\ 2nx+4x+7 & =-4x+5+4x \\ 2nx+4x+7 & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we subtract $7$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2nx+4x+7 & =5 \\ 2nx+4x+7-7 & =5-7 \\ 2nx+4x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we factor $x$ on the left-hand side. This gives

$$
(2n + 4)x  = -2.
$$

Notice that this equation is now in the form $ax = b{:}$

$$
\underbrace{(2n + 4)}_{a}x  = \underbrace{-2}_{b}
$$

Therefore, the equation has no solution if

$$
2n + 4= 0.
$$

Solving this for $n,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2n+4 & =0 \\ 2n+4-4 & =0-4 \\ 2n & =-4 \\ \frac{2n}{2} & =\frac{-4}{2} \\ n & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186051079} {:db/id 17592186477074} {:db/id 17592186204598 :question/id #uuid "c5eb239a-6da7-5d84-946d-c53824d57aa5" :question/math-academy-id "q-287677"} {:db/id 17592186204599 :question/id #uuid "13915c55-7c7c-53b4-adee-86cf0ce79ae1" :question/math-academy-id "q-287678"} {:db/id 17592186297205 :question/id #uuid "6cf4ece6-fb8b-5a6f-963d-f97832f4331b" :question/math-academy-id "q-288662" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186204092 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d63847ef-6360-50b5-b585-9084140b2d67" :knowledge-point/title "Solving For an Unknown Parameter - :topic/math-academy-id 5572} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186205035 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205174 :tutorial/content "Some linear equations can have **no solutions.** This means there is no value of $x$ that can be substituted into the equation to give a true statement.

For example, let's consider the following equation:

$$
x+1 = x
$$

Let's attempt to solve this equation. We start by subtracting $x$ from both sides.

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x \\ x+1\,-\,x & =x\,-\,x \\ (x-x)+1 & =(x-x) \\ 0+1 & =0 \\ 1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the final equation, $1=0,$ is always **false**. In other words, there is no value of $x$ that we can substitute to make the equation true. 

Therefore, our equation has no solutions." :tutorial/id #uuid "ae552721-c050-5d83-9cfc-347accbc894b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 11390 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1b8a4ffe-a6bc-5748-9925-775d621ef0ae" :step/math-academy-id 476517 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205036}} {:db/id 17592186205036 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204089 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203852 :question/id #uuid "fd07ad0f-548a-5569-84de-d658a88c4b9c" :question/math-academy-id "e-17087"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d6226fdb-ee73-5a78-87d5-9d6a988a9eb4" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048213}] :knowledge-point/question-generator {:db/id 17592186476177} :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204600} {:db/id 17592186204601} {:db/id 17592186297172} {:db/id 17592186297173} {:db/id 17592186297174} {:db/id 17592186297175} {:db/id 17592186297176}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying an Equation With No Solutions"} :step/id #uuid "2a517a1e-2402-5834-92c6-d387d20f3740" :step/math-academy-id 476518 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205037}} {:db/id 17592186205037 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205208 :tutorial/content "In general, suppose we have an equation in the variable $x$ of the form 

$$
ax = b,
$$

where 

- $a$ and $b$ are constants, and

- $b$ is *not* equal to zero, which we write as $b \neq 0.$

Then, if $a = 0,$ the equation has **no solutions.**

Indeed, by substituting $a = 0$ into $ax=b,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}ax & =b \\ (0)x & =b \\ 0 & =b\end{aligned}
$$

which is a *contradiction* (i.e., a statement that's always false) because we were told that $b \neq 0.$ Therefore, the equation has no solution." :tutorial/id #uuid "8a5cc3be-1b56-5e46-8944-f75697b65b59" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13428 :tutorial/title "Conditions for an Equation To Have No Solutions"} :step/id #uuid "a4d784bb-4dc8-51b7-9c57-1caf81eeaf95" :step/math-academy-id 476521 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205038}} {:db/id 17592186205038 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205207 :tutorial/content "Consider the equation in the variable $x,$ given by

$$
7qx = -5,
$$

where $q$ is a constant. Given that this equation has no solutions, what is the value of $q?$

Notice that this equation is in the form $ax = b{:}$ 

$$
\underbrace{7q}_{\large a} \ x = \underbrace{-5}_{\large b}
$$

In this case,

$$
a = 7q, \qquad b = -5.
$$

We know that an equation of the form $ax=b$ with $b \neq 0$ has no solutions when $a = 0.$
Therefore, the equation has no solution if

$$
7q = 0.
$$

Solving this for $q,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}7q & =0 \\ \frac{7q}{7} & =\frac{0}{7} \\ q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the equation $7qx = -5$ has no solutions if $q = 0.$

**Note:** The constant $q$ in this problem is sometimes called a **parameter.**

Similarly, the equation

\[
(p + 3)x = -9,
\]

where [math]p[/math] is a constant, is an equation in the form [math]ax = b{:}[/math] 

\[
\underbrace{(p + 3)}_{\large a} \ x = \underbrace{-9}_{\large b},
\]

In this case,

\[
a = p + 3, \qquad b = -9.
\]

Therefore, the equation has no solution if
\[
p + 3 = 0.
\]

Solving this for [math]p,[/math] we get
\begin{align*}
p + 3 & = 0 \\[5pt]
p & = -3.
\end{align*}

So, the equation has no solution when [math]p=-3.[/math]" :tutorial/id #uuid "d31382b3-ae61-5a9e-a3bf-53f71f939a5d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13402 :tutorial/title "Problems Involving Unknown Parameters"} :step/id #uuid "15db0382-7d51-5840-b3da-75384a89354d" :step/math-academy-id 476522 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205039}} {:db/id 17592186205039 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204090 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203853 :question/id #uuid "cba9196c-fdc3-594d-a1ad-948cf75bd366" :question/math-academy-id "e-17213"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c0e7426e-553d-5f20-811f-15f3a5ea0056" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204596} {:db/id 17592186204602} {:db/id 17592186297177} {:db/id 17592186297178} {:db/id 17592186297179} {:db/id 17592186297197}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving For an Unknown Parameter"} :step/id #uuid "8211e280-4fa1-564c-9189-09c44ee53dde" :step/math-academy-id 476523 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205040}} {:db/id 17592186205040 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204091 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203878 :question/id #uuid "5ee14499-89b0-59a3-9f13-b0a00c0e518d" :question/math-academy-id "e-18853"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ba644b27-7245-5b7b-8cd6-2493836a7d03" :knowledge-point/question-generator {:db/id 17592186477042} :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204597} {:db/id 17592186204603} {:db/id 17592186297201} {:db/id 17592186297202} {:db/id 17592186297203} {:db/id 17592186297204} {:db/id 17592186477030} {:db/id 17592186477031} {:db/id 17592186477034} {:db/id 17592186477035} {:db/id 17592186477039}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving For an Unknown Parameter - \begin{aligned}ax & =b \\ (0)x & =b \\ 0 & =b\end{aligned}
$$

which is a *contradiction* (i.e., a statement that's always false) because we were told that $b \neq 0.$ Therefore, the equation has no solution." :tutorial/id #uuid "8a5cc3be-1b56-5e46-8944-f75697b65b59" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13428 :tutorial/title "Conditions for an Equation To Have No Solutions"} :step/id #uuid "a4d784bb-4dc8-51b7-9c57-1caf81eeaf95" :step/math-academy-id 476521 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205038}} {:db/id 17592186205208 :tutorial/content "In general, suppose we have an equation in the variable $x$ of the form 

$$
ax = b,
$$

where 

- $a$ and $b$ are constants, and

- $b$ is *not* equal to zero, which we write as $b \neq 0.$

Then, if $a = 0,$ the equation has **no solutions.**

Indeed, by substituting $a = 0$ into $ax=b,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}ax & =b \\ (0)x & =b \\ 0 & =b\end{aligned}
$$

which is a *contradiction* (i.e., a statement that's always false) because we were told that $b \neq 0.$ Therefore, the equation has no solution." :tutorial/id #uuid "8a5cc3be-1b56-5e46-8944-f75697b65b59" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13428 :tutorial/title "Conditions for an Equation To Have No Solutions"} {:db/id 17592186205038 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205207 :tutorial/content "Consider the equation in the variable $x,$ given by

$$
7qx = -5,
$$

where $q$ is a constant. Given that this equation has no solutions, what is the value of $q?$

Notice that this equation is in the form $ax = b{:}$ 

$$
\underbrace{7q}_{\large a} \ x = \underbrace{-5}_{\large b}
$$

In this case,

$$
a = 7q, \qquad b = -5.
$$

We know that an equation of the form $ax=b$ with $b \neq 0$ has no solutions when $a = 0.$
Therefore, the equation has no solution if

$$
7q = 0.
$$

Solving this for $q,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}7q & =0 \\ \frac{7q}{7} & =\frac{0}{7} \\ q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the equation $7qx = -5$ has no solutions if $q = 0.$

**Note:** The constant $q$ in this problem is sometimes called a **parameter.**

Similarly, the equation

\[
(p + 3)x = -9,
\]

where [math]p[/math] is a constant, is an equation in the form [math]ax = b{:}[/math] 

\[
\underbrace{(p + 3)}_{\large a} \ x = \underbrace{-9}_{\large b},
\]

In this case,

\[
a = p + 3, \qquad b = -9.
\]

Therefore, the equation has no solution if
\[
p + 3 = 0.
\]

Solving this for [math]p,[/math] we get
\begin{align*}
p + 3 & = 0 \\[5pt]
p & = -3.
\end{align*}

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We use the central difference approximation

Approximate the rate at which the temperature of the engine increases when $t = 3$ using a central difference approximation with step size $h=1.$" :question/worked-solution "We use the central difference approximation

$$
T'(t) \approx \dfrac{T(t+h) - T(t-h)}{2h},
$$

 

at the time $t=3$ with step size $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(3) & ≈\frac{T(3+1)-T(3-1)}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{T(4)-T(2)}{2} \\  & =\frac{60-30}{2} \\  & =\frac{30}{2} \\  & =15.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of temperature increase is approximately $15^{\circ}$ per minute."} {:db/id 17592186078960 :question/id #uuid "79273943-9e5e-5a15-9faf-8c6d22ca7bd8" :question/math-academy-id - The forward difference approximation computes the rate of change between the point $x$ and the point $x+h,$ which is a step of $h$ units forward.

f'(x)  \approx \dfrac{f(x+h)- f(x)}{h}
$$

$$

$$

$$
f'(x)  \approx \dfrac{f(x+h)- f(x-h)}{2h}
$$

17592186045493} :db/id 17592186153880}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{3{x}^{2}+4}{5},\,0<x<1
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{11}{20},$ compute $\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1].$

*Hint: You may assume that $\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$*" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1] & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+\text{E}[1] \\  & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+1\end{aligned}
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the third raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{3}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{3{x}^{2}+4}{5})\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{3}{5}{x}^{5}+\frac{4}{5}{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{10}{x}^{6}+\frac{1}{5}{x}^{4})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=\frac{11}{20}$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{3}]=\frac{3}{10}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1] & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+1 \\  & =2\cdot \frac{11}{20}-\frac{3}{10}+1 \\  & =\frac{11}{10}-\frac{3}{10}+1 \\  & =\frac{9}{5}.\end{aligned}

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{2x},\,{e}^{-2}<x<1
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}},$ compute $\text{E}[4{X}^{2}-2X].$

*Hint: You may assume that $\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$*" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[4{X}^{2}-2X]=4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-2\text{E}[X]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{{e}^{-2}}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{{e}^{-2}}^{1}\frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}\,|}_{{e}^{-2}}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[4{X}^{2}-2X] & =4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-2\text{E}[X] \\  & =4(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}})-2(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}) \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}-1+\frac{1}{{e}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186427367 :question/id #uuid "78882664-5ca1-5d0e-9798-9cca3f283762" :question/math-academy-id "q-90451"} {:db/id 17592186427369 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{2},\,1<x<3
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=2,$ compute $\text{E}[5X-3{X}^{2}].$

*Hint: You may assume that $\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$*" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[5X-3{X}^{2}]=5\text{E}[X]-3\text{E}[{X}^{2}]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}\,|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{13}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=2$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=\frac{13}{3}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[5X-3{X}^{2}] & =5\text{E}[X]-3\text{E}[{X}^{2}] \\  & =5\cdot 2-3\cdot \frac{13}{3} \\  & =10-13 \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186434428 :question/id #uuid "fc2748a6-b91a-5b23-b40c-5cede2d8d71d" :question/math-academy-id "q-90394"} {:db/id 17592186479144 :question/id #uuid "f6cddda8-c777-5283-b03a-3671533a782a" :question/math-academy-id "q-131153" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1cfd005b-75a8-5b0f-ba56-4a0ed93ab33a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186478604} {:answer/id #uuid "22afcee8-e19d-562c-b205-332bc6a88919" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186478613} {:answer/id #uuid "7a90c263-2858-513a-872f-0ae63784d35a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186478741} {:answer/id #uuid "edf857b5-69b2-5c68-8336-4b0f3c36ec60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186478931} {:answer/id #uuid "ff85e4b7-ab02-503c-8793-d2b775c75049" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186478958}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186478958} :answer-field/id #uuid "623ea09b-af47-50f2-9745-0713c7359869" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186478997}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[10-4{X}^{2}].$

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[10-4{X}^{2}]=10-4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2\,\text{d}x \\  & =2x\,{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=2$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[10-4{X}^{2}] & =10-4\text{E}[{X}^{2}] \\  & =10-4\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186157394 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186156995 :question/id #uuid "292610ec-9c27-590d-b207-c76adc959d55" :question/math-academy-id "e-10528"} :knowledge-point/id function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S.$

The values $\textrm{E}[X]$ and $\textrm{E}[X^2]$ are called the **first moment** and **second moment** of $X,$ respectively. 

Recall that the first moment $\textrm{E}[X]$ is also called the *expected value* of $X$ and is computed as follows:

$$
\displaystyle \textrm{E}[X] = \int_S x \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x
$$

To find second moment $\textrm{E}[X^2],$ the expected value of the the random variable $X^2,$ we simply substitute $x^2$ for $x$ in the formula above, as follows:

$$
\displaystyle \textrm{E}[X^2] = \int_S x^2 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x
$$

Let's compute the second moment $\textrm{E}[X^2]$ of the continuous random variable $X$ with the probability density function 

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}, \qquad 0 \leq x \leq 1.
$$

We compute the expected value of $X^2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{5/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(\frac{2}{7}{x}^{7/2}){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(\frac{2}{7}-0) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2847fd82-e842-5ae8-889a-66f29c0442ec" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6591 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3dc1ae12-0989-5596-8114-7d74427919d2" :step/math-academy-id {:db/id 17592186158294 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158563 :tutorial/content "It's also possible to define higher moments. For example, $\textrm{E}[X^3]$ is the **third moment** of the random variable $X.$

Notice the pattern:

- $\displaystyle \textrm{E}[X] = \int_S x \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x$ is the *first* moment

- $\displaystyle \textrm{E}[X^2] = \int_S x^2 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x$ is the *second* moment

- $\displaystyle \textrm{E}[X^3] = \int_S x^3 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x$ is the *third* moment

and so on. In general, the **$n$th moment** is given by

$$
\textrm{E}[X^n] = \int_S x^n \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Finally, note that 

$$
\textrm{E}[X], \quad \textrm{E}[X^2], \quad \textrm{E}[X^3], \quad \ldots
$$

are sometimes referred to as the first, second, and third **raw moments**. This is because it's possible to define other types of moments.

In general, $\textrm{E}[X^n]$ can be called either the $n$th *moment* or $n$th *raw moment*." :tutorial/id #uuid "e3527d5e-b0d3-5d76-aa5f-5bc7ffcfd66b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6592 :tutorial/title "Higher Moments"} :step/id #uuid "9fb3611b-a9ba-58f4-9159-00a7c9b29393" :step/math-academy-id 39757 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158293}}] :activity/title "Moments of Continuous Random Variables" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186157533} {:db/id 17592186158290 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158562 :tutorial/content "Suppose $X$ is a continuous random variable with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S.$

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2847fd82-e842-5ae8-889a-66f29c0442ec" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6591 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186158292 :step/content {:db/id 17592186157394 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186156995 :question/id #uuid "292610ec-9c27-590d-b207-c76adc959d55" :question/math-academy-id "e-10528"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bada6a7f-c02e-51cd-8ea2-0594a94648a1" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048516} {:db/id 17592186049801}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186157602} {:db/id 17592186157603} {:db/id 17592186427360} {:db/id 17592186427361} {:db/id 17592186427368} {:db/id 17592186427372} {:db/id 17592186427373} {:db/id 17592186434425}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Second Moment of a Random Variable"} :step/id #uuid "08325c1e-fe0c-5a7b-b6e5-8f27c2951461" :step/math-academy-id 39755 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158294}} {:db/id 17592186158291 :step/content {:db/id 17592186157393 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186156994 :question/id #uuid "65957407-b302-51c5-93d9-0f71f3517362" :question/math-academy-id "e-10527"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f9c799d6-e3fe-5b78-986d-f2068b2db058" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050775}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186157606} {:db/id 17592186157991} {:db/id 17592186427364} {:db/id 17592186427367} {:db/id 17592186427369} {:db/id 17592186427370} {:db/id 17592186427371} {:db/id 17592186434427} {:db/id 17592186434428} {:db/id 17592186479144}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Mean of a Transformed Random Variable"} :step/id #uuid "897313ee-485e-51e5-8fec-b665d482b874" :step/math-academy-id 39754} {:db/id 17592186158294 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158563 :tutorial/content "It's also possible to define higher moments. For example, $\textrm{E}[X^3]$ is the **third moment** of the random variable $X.$

Notice the pattern:

- $\displaystyle \textrm{E}[X] = \int_S x \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x$ is the *first* moment

- $\displaystyle \textrm{E}[X^2] = \int_S x^2 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x$ is the *second* moment

- $\displaystyle \textrm{E}[X^3] = \int_S x^3 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x$ is the *third* moment

and so on. In general, the **$n$th moment** is given by

$$
\textrm{E}[X^n] = \int_S x^n \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Finally, note that 

$$
\textrm{E}[X], \quad \textrm{E}[X^2], \quad \textrm{E}[X^3], \quad \ldots
$$

are sometimes referred to as the first, second, and third **raw moments**. This is because it's possible to define other types of moments.

In general, $\textrm{E}[X^n]$ can be called either the $n$th *moment* or $n$th *raw moment*." :tutorial/id #uuid "e3527d5e-b0d3-5d76-aa5f-5bc7ffcfd66b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6592 :tutorial/title "Higher Moments"} :step/id #uuid "9fb3611b-a9ba-58f4-9159-00a7c9b29393" :step/math-academy-id 39757 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158293}} {:db/id 17592186158293 :step/content {:db/id 17592186157395 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186156996 :question/id #uuid "4c5666a4-f477-5b1a-8d17-1e2aa594863f" :question/math-academy-id "e-10529"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "88bd32d5-4a84-58b3-a3e9-73bf32cb5e4f" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186157604} {:db/id 17592186157605} {:db/id 17592186427362} {:db/id 17592186427363} {:db/id 17592186427365} {:db/id 17592186427366} {:db/id 17592186434426} {:db/id 17592186479070} {:db/id 17592186479115}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Higher Moments of a Random Variable"} :step/id #uuid "bce87273-1a01-58a6-825f-736ef62ef788" :step/math-academy-id 39756 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158291}} {:db/id 17592186158563 :tutorial/content "It's also possible to define higher moments. $$
f(x)=\frac{1}{4}(1-x),\,-2\le x\le 0.
$$

Calculate $\text{E}[{X}^{3}].$" :question/worked-solution "For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we compute the third raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{3}] & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{x}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{4}(1-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-2}^{0}({x}^{3}-{x}^{4})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}-\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}){|}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(0-[4+\frac{32}{5}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(-\frac{52}{5}) \\  & =-\frac{13}{5}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "121da9a3-a27d-57e3-b7b6-52d9b4081634" :step/next {:db/id 17592186479157}} {:db/id 17592186479151 :step/content {:db/id 17592186427364 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33cb4776-7d73-5e89-be66-3abb80c22cd1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}" :db/id 17592186427291} {:answer/id #uuid "5d5bf664-a18f-566d-a4f7-3bd738b55f2b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\frac{1}{e}" :db/id 17592186427301} {:answer/id #uuid "74d74ac0-e401-549d-95e1-5b551db31568" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}+2" :db/id 17592186427309} {:answer/id #uuid "aa2240d8-61b4-5dec-86e4-1ecedc83ab1c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{e}" :db/id 17592186427322} {:answer/id #uuid "ce1156f5-fddd-5d6b-adf1-9732ee27312f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{e}-1" :db/id 17592186427333}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186427291} :answer-field/id #uuid "62e8ebaf-8a75-5cb6-8621-5bcf5f7ac9e4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186427348}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "63bcffd8-dbf0-5c48-8ca6-56531c05d1c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-131141" :question/problem "The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{2x},\,{e}^{-2}<x<1
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}},$ compute $\text{E}[4{X}^{2}-2X].$

*Hint: You may assume that $\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$*" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[4{X}^{2}-2X]=4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-2\text{E}[X]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{{e}^{-2}}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{{e}^{-2}}^{1}\frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}\,|}_{{e}^{-2}}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[4{X}^{2}-2X] & =4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-2\text{E}[X] \\  & =4(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}})-2(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}) \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}-1+\frac{1}{{e}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1ec8cc12-b2a4-5daf-96fd-1e378052ed2d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186479152}} {:db/id 17592186479152 :step/content {:db/id 17592186479144 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1cfd005b-75a8-5b0f-ba56-4a0ed93ab33a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186478604} {:answer/id #uuid "22afcee8-e19d-562c-b205-332bc6a88919" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186478613} {:answer/id #uuid "7a90c263-2858-513a-872f-0ae63784d35a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186478741} {:answer/id #uuid "edf857b5-69b2-5c68-8336-4b0f3c36ec60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186478931} {:answer/id #uuid "ff85e4b7-ab02-503c-8793-d2b775c75049" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186478958}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186478958} :answer-field/id #uuid "623ea09b-af47-50f2-9745-0713c7359869" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186478997}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "f6cddda8-c777-5283-b03a-3671533a782a" :question/math-academy-id "q-131153" :question/problem "Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[10-4{X}^{2}].$

$$
f(x)=\frac{2}{{x}^{2}},\,1<x<2
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[10-4{X}^{2}]=10-4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2\,\text{d}x \\  & =2x\,{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=2$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[10-4{X}^{2}] & =10-4\text{E}[{X}^{2}] \\  & =10-4\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "46c499f6-0d50-5bd9-9f52-26ed8cb8ebb6" :step/next {:db/id 17592186479153}} {:db/id 17592186479153 :step/content {:db/id 17592186157606 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a69b927d-fd51-516f-aae0-cf0da09a7720" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{5}" :db/id 17592186153881} {:answer/id #uuid "e3ba8dfc-c937-598b-a9a5-dc59f7c01e72" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{10}" :db/id 17592186153882} {:answer/id #uuid "eb402453-8e9e-5d3c-a06e-96fbfc84d9da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{5}" :db/id 17592186153883} {:answer/id #uuid "f418ec1e-ed9d-5bce-a47f-762f1c808098" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{19}{10}" :db/id 17592186153884} {:answer/id #uuid "63a0df93-12b0-5a94-8153-cab57c777d0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{17}{10}" :db/id 17592186153885}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186153883} :answer-field/id #uuid "07e9af8f-c53a-563f-b1d5-c1fb676708fa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186153880}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "d40b16f4-c022-5679-aaee-aa1be46926d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-149708" :question/problem "The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{3{x}^{2}+4}{5},\,0<x<1
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{11}{20},$ compute $\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1].$

*Hint: You may assume that $\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$*" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1] & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+\text{E}[1] \\  & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+1\end{aligned}
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the third raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{3}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{3{x}^{2}+4}{5})\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{3}{5}{x}^{5}+\frac{4}{5}{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{10}{x}^{6}+\frac{1}{5}{x}^{4})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=\frac{11}{20}$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{3}]=\frac{3}{10}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1] & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+1 \\  & =2\cdot \frac{11}{20}-\frac{3}{10}+1 \\  & =\frac{11}{10}-\frac{3}{10}+1 \\  & =\frac{9}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "473a0974-6e51-5843-94d7-0cf17d7cd776" :step/next {:db/id 17592186479149}} {:db/id 17592186479157 :step/content {:db/id 17592186479070 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1370ffbd-2eab-5260-a0b4-0bf5d3cdb6db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{5}" :db/id 17592186478582} {:answer/id #uuid "7f3f6cb5-53fa-5af5-81d3-830801107641" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{17}{9}" :db/id 17592186478750} {:answer/id #uuid "82d2a8f9-d415-5d71-a7d9-fe699cab072f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{21}{25}" :db/id 17592186478758} {:answer/id #uuid "bedb09af-8e03-5cb2-a39f-8ac2f91ce3a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{19}{16}" :db/id 17592186478867} {:answer/id #uuid "e89460a9-557b-5055-9a71-6a052e322419" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{11}{6}" :db/id 17592186478921}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186478867} :answer-field/id #uuid "aded51f8-58f0-5888-884c-244971621142" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186479026}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "2317ff10-80a3-5747-858a-863cca47fbc9" :question/math-academy-id "q-152922" :question/problem "A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function 

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}, & 0\le x<1 \\ \frac{1}{{x}^{5}}, & x\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate $\text{E}[{X}^{3}].$" :question/worked-solution "For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we compute the third raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{3}] & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\cdot \frac{3}{4}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{5}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{16}\,{x}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{1}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{1}{x}){|}_{1}^{a} \\  & =\frac{3}{16}(1-0)+{lim}_{a\to \infty }(1-\frac{1}{a}) \\  & =\frac{3}{16}+(1-0) \\  & =\frac{19}{16}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{{e}^{-2}}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{{e}^{-2}}^{1}\frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}\,|}_{{e}^{-2}}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[4{X}^{2}-2X] & =4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-2\text{E}[X] \\  & =4(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}})-2(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}) \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}-1+\frac{1}{{e}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}.\end{aligned}

"The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:
